# Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys {#sec-heterosis}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
ctx  <- simulate_data(book_cfg)
L    <- simulate_lines(book_cfg)
pool <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(book_cfg$n_pool_A, book_cfg$n_pool_B))
P    <- pool_freqs(L / 2, pool)
pA   <- P["A", ]
pB   <- P["B", ]
nA   <- book_cfg$n_pool_A
U    <- L[seq_len(nA), ] / 2
V    <- L[nA + seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_B), ] / 2
set.seed(4)
d    <- rgamma(ctx$m, 2, 4)
# Named vector -> two-column table (quantity, value). `sig = TRUE` formats each
# value to `digits` significant digits, so a residual of 1e-16 is not rounded to 0.
kv <- function(x, digits = 4, sig = FALSE) {
  data.frame(quantity = names(x),
             value = if (sig) unname(vapply(x, format, "", digits = digits)) else fmt(unname(x), digits))
}
```


Since @sec-subdivided this book has repeated a claim without proving it: that the
divergence between the heterotic pools is the engine of heterosis, and is therefore
to be maintained rather than minimised. @sec-catalogue will decompose diversity on
that basis and @sec-stages will build a monitoring panel around it. The claim has
carried a lot of weight for an assertion.

The chapters before this one announce what it supplies. @sec-hybrid-programme
states the identity numerically and hands its derivation here
(@sec-heterosis-identity) together with the dominance part of the combining-ability
model of @eq-hp-gca-sca (@sec-heterosis-gca-sca); @sec-coancestry introduces the
dominance effects $d_k$ and the heterosis $H_i$ of @eq-het-value, derived below;
@sec-subdivided gives the partition the identity is stated in
(@tbl-keystone); and @sec-response states two facts about combining ability --
without dominance a line's GCA is the same against any tester set, with dominance
it is evaluated at the other pool's frequencies -- and refers the derivation to
@sec-heterosis-gca-sca.

This chapter derives the claim, and then corrects it. The derivation is short and the
identity is exact, under the conditions stated at each use: flat dominance,
inbred parents and the complete $A \times B$ factorial. It has two halves. At
a given $GD_T$ (total gene diversity) -- the quantity the $\alpha$ budget constrains (@tbl-keystone) --
expected heterosis is $GD_T + GD_{BS}$ (@eq-het-theta-ab), so a loss of
$GD_{BS}$ (the between-pool component) is a loss of expected heterosis, one for one: that is the sense in which
the divergence is *maintained*. The correction concerns the other half: the
reading of the identity that this chapter corrects is *push the pools apart and you
will get more heterosis*. It is put here as the natural reading; it is not
attributed to any author and no source is cited for it. That reading is false. Under neutral divergence expected heterosis does not move, in
expectation over the draw of the pools (@eq-het-bn-total), and the sweep of
@sec-heterosis-flat, one draw per row, is consistent with it.

The chapter then goes one step past the mean. Expected heterosis is what a pool
pair is worth on average; what a breeder selects on is how heterosis is
*distributed* across the crosses of the factorial. Those are different questions
with different answers, and the second one is where general and specific combining
ability (GCA, SCA) come from.

The derivations come first and @sec-heterosis-protocol turns them into the eight
steps that compute them on a real programme's data, with the check and the
failure mode of each one. Read that section first if the question is what to run
rather than why it holds.

The data come from `simulate_lines()` and `simulate_data()`, drawn with the
generator @sec-simulating-crosses builds (in the Simulation part that follows),
and the `fst` sweep of @sec-heterosis-flat redraws the pools from it;
`pool_complementarity()` supplies the three complementarity columns of the S1 panel
(`s1_monitor()`; S1 is defined in @tbl-hp-stages and the panel in @sec-stages).

## Three premises {#sec-heterosis-premises}

Three premises carry everything below. They are stated here once, because every
result in the chapter uses all three and two of them are restrictive.

**Parents are fully inbred.** Every parent line is homozygous at every locus, so
an F1's marker row is the average of its two parents' rows and a locus is
heterozygous in the F1 exactly when the parents differ. This is what makes the
additive effects cancel from the mid-parent difference and what makes `GD_WI`
zero. Note that this is a property of the *programme*, not of the mating system:
the programme modelled here is that of an allogamous, maize-type crop with two
heterotic pools under reciprocal recurrent selection (a modelling choice; no source
for the heterotic-group system is cited in this chapter). Doubled-haploid (DH)
induction or selfing to fixation is what delivers homozygous parents from it. Nothing here transfers to a programme
crossing non-inbred parents (an inter-population cross, a synthetic, parents selfed once)
without re-derivation, and @sec-heterosis-step1 measures how large the error is
if the formulae below are applied anyway: a multiple of the true gain, not a few
per cent.

**The genotypic model is dominance within loci and additivity between them.**
There is no epistatic term anywhere below: the genotypic value is a sum over
loci, $H_i$ is a sum of per-locus indicators, and the combining-ability expansion
of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is bilinear only because no term couples two loci.
@labroo2021 review epistasis alongside dominance as a proposed mechanism for
heterosis; this model excludes it, and no result below should be read as evidence
about it. What $d_k$ does absorb is every *within-locus* story, as @sec-heterosis-dk-meaning sets out.

**The marker panel is the set of dominance loci.** $d_k$ is indexed by the same
$k$ as the markers, so every locus carrying dominance is genotyped and the
frequency statistics are computed on exactly the loci that generate heterosis.
This is the strongest assumption of the three, and it is the one that carries the
distance results of @sec-heterosis-distance. A real panel tags causal loci
through linkage disequilibrium rather than containing them, which weakens every
statement below about markers predicting heterosis but does not change the
algebra, since the algebra is written over whatever set $k$ indexes. A related
choice: every number below that depends on $d$ (the correlation with marker
distance, the alignment factor, the SCA shares) uses one draw of $d_k$ from a gamma
distribution (shape 2, rate 4, seed 4), positive at every locus and the same at
every pool pair and scale, which is an illustrative assumption and not an
estimate. The chapter does not vary it; the algebra holds for any $d$, the
magnitudes do not.

## The dominance model, minimally

### The one-locus scale

The classical parameterisation puts the origin at the midpoint of the two
homozygotes: one homozygote is worth $+a$, the other $-a$, and the heterozygote
$d$. Under random mating at frequency $p$, with $q = 1 - p$, the population mean
is [@falconer1996, Ch. 7]

$$M = a\,(p - q) + 2pq\,d$$ {#eq-het-mean-one-locus}

The first term is the additive contribution, and the mid-parent of any cross
already carries it. The second is the dominance contribution. It is the only part
of $M$ that depends on how many heterozygotes there are, and therefore the only
part a cross can add over its own mid-parent.

::: {.callout-note}
## $a$ is a scale, not a quantity this chapter computes

The symbols in @eq-het-mean-one-locus are the textbook ones. This book's additive marker
effects are $\beta_k$ (estimated in @sec-genomic-prediction, later), and its $\alpha$ is the
diversity-loss statistic of @sec-catalogue, not the classical average effect of a
substitution. The per-locus $a_k$ reappears below and never as a
result: in the genotypic-value model (@eq-het-genotypic-value) used to show that it cancels, in the
additive part of the GCA of the cross mean (@sec-heterosis-gca-sca) and of the two-way layout of
@sec-heterosis-protocol, and, written without the index, in the definition of overdominance as
$|d| > |a|$ and in the average effect of a substitution $a + d(q - p)$ (@sec-heterosis-gca-average).
No quantity this chapter reports depends on it.
:::

### What $d_k$ is, and what it is not {#sec-heterosis-dk-meaning}


$d_k$ is the **dominance effect** at locus $k$: the *functional* dominance, the
departure of the heterozygote from the homozygote midpoint (the heterozygote value
on the $a$, $d$, $-a$ scale of @eq-het-mean-one-locus). It is a property of the
locus. It does not move when allele frequencies move. This chapter,
@sec-hybrid-programme, @sec-coancestry, @sec-subdivided and @sec-response call $d_k$ the dominance
effect and nothing else; the phrase *dominance deviation* is kept for the object
that follows. Other chapters (@sec-genomic-era among them) still use the older
name for $d_k$; it is a difference of wording and not a different quantity.

Fisher's *statistical* dominance deviation [@fisher1918; @falconer1996, Ch. 7]
is a different object: the residual left after projecting genotypic values onto
the best additive model **in a particular population**. It is a property of the population as much as of the
locus, and it changes when frequencies change.

Both appear in this chapter, and keeping them apart is the whole trick.
$d_k$ is the input. The specific combining ability of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is
the statistical dominance deviation that a given $d_k$ *induces* over a given pair
of pools. One is a constant; the other is an answer that depends on where the
pools happen to sit.

The distinction also buys the model what generality it has, and marks where that
generality stops. Dominance, overdominance (a heterozygote outside both
homozygotes, $|d| > |a|$) and pseudo-overdominance (two dominant favourable
alleles in repulsion phase, too close for any marker to separate) are three
different biological stories, and @labroo2021 review the evidence for each. At
marker resolution they are the same arithmetic: a locus at which the F1 gains
something the mid-parent does not. A single $d_k$ absorbs all three, and nothing
below can distinguish them -- nor needs to. Epistasis is the fourth story on
@labroo2021's list and $d_k$ does not absorb it, because a single per-locus
number cannot represent a term that depends on two loci at once. That is the
second premise of @sec-heterosis-premises (dominance within loci, additivity between), and it is an exclusion rather than an approximation.

### The mid-parent difference

Code a genotype by $x_k \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}$, the frequency of the reference allele
within the individual, and take the genotypic value to be the additive part plus
the dominance effect at every heterozygous locus:

$$G(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_k a_k\,(2x_k - 1) + \sum_k d_k\,\mathbb{1}\{x_k = 0.5\}$$ {#eq-het-genotypic-value}

The parents are fully inbred, so each is homozygous at every locus and the F1's
row is the average of its two parents' rows. The additive part is linear in
$\mathbf{x}$, so the two parents' additive values average exactly to the F1's own
and cancel from the mid-parent difference. What survives is the dominance
effect at the loci where the F1 is heterozygous:

$$H_i = \sum_k d_k \, \mathbb{1}\{x_{ik} = 0.5\}$$ {#eq-het-value}

The additive effects never appear. That is the result, not an omission, and it is
why `heterosis_value()` takes no additive-effect argument:

```{r}
cat(deparse(heterosis_value), sep = "\n")
```

Against the literal oracle of @sec-verification, which loops over loci and
compares the two parents' genotypes one at a time, on 25 hybrids drawn at random
from the factorial (so that both pools' line indexing is exercised; @tbl-het-oracle-gap):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-oracle-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute difference between `heterosis_value()` and the literal oracle `ref_heterosis()` over 25 hybrids drawn at random from the full factorial (seed 12), in units of $d$."
set.seed(12)                        # 25 random hybrids, not the first 25 rows
i25 <- sample(ctx$N, 25)
# ref_heterosis() takes the 0/2 line matrix L; the line-level functions of the
# package take 0/1 (see the protocol section)
oracle_gap <- max(abs(heterosis_value(ctx$X[i25, , drop = FALSE], d) -
                      ref_heterosis(L, ctx$ped[i25, ], d)))
stopifnot(oracle_gap < 1e-9)
kv(c(max_abs_difference = oracle_gap), sig = TRUE)

```

The cancellation is worth seeing directly. Draw additive effects at random, score
a real F1 and its two parents under $G(\mathbf{x})$, and subtract (@tbl-het-cancellation):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-cancellation
#| tbl-cap: "Mid-parent difference of one F1 (hybrid 7) scored under $G(\\mathbf{x})$ of @eq-het-genotypic-value with random additive effects $a_k$ (seed 9), beside its dominance value $H_i$ from `heterosis_value()` (@eq-het-value), in units of $d$."
set.seed(9)                         # the cancellation is exact for any a; seed it anyway
a   <- rnorm(ctx$m, 0, 0.2)
val <- function(x) sum(a * (2 * x - 1)) + sum(d * (x == 0.5))
i   <- 7
mid <- (val(L[ctx$ped$a[i], ] / 2) + val(L[ctx$ped$b[i], ] / 2)) / 2
kv(c(mid_parent_difference = val(ctx$X[i, ]) - mid,
     heterosis_value       = heterosis_value(ctx$X[i, , drop = FALSE], d)), 6)
```

The additive effects entered the first number and cancelled out of it; they never
entered the second.

## Expected heterosis over a pool pair

Write $p_{Ak}$ and $p_{Bk}$ for the reference-allele frequencies at locus $k$ in
the two pools, each computed over that pool's lines. A locus is heterozygous in
the F1 when the two gametes carry different alleles, which for a cross drawn at
random between the pools happens with probability $p_A(1 - p_B) + (1 - p_A)p_B$.
The expected heterosis over all $A \times B$ crosses therefore follows from the
pool frequencies alone:

$$\mathbb{E}[H] = \sum_k d_k \left[\, p_{A k} + p_{B k} - 2 p_{A k} p_{B k} \right]$$ {#eq-het-expected}

The candidate set here *is* the full factorial, every $A \times B$ pairing
exactly once, and the frequencies are the means of those same lines. The closed form is then the mean of the realised values as an identity rather than an
approximation, and the residual is at machine precision (@tbl-het-expected-identity):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-expected-identity
#| tbl-cap: "Absolute difference between the closed form `heterosis_expected()` (@eq-het-expected) and the mean of `heterosis_value()` over the 625 crosses of the full factorial, in units of $d$."
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d),
                           mean(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)))))
kv(c(abs_difference = abs(heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d) - mean(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)))),
   sig = TRUE)
```

That is a mean over $N =$ `r ctx$N` crosses, and a mean is not a ranking. Hold on
to the question of how the individual crosses are spread around it;
@sec-heterosis-gca-sca answers it exactly.

## The identity {#sec-heterosis-identity}

Now split the bracket. Writing $\bar p = (p_A + p_B)/2$ and $y = p_A - p_B$, the
per-locus F1 heterozygosity separates exactly:

$$p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B \;=\; \underbrace{2 \bar p (1 - \bar p)}_{\text{shared}}
                            \;+\; \underbrace{y^2 / 2}_{\text{divergence}}$$ {#eq-het-split}

The first term is the heterozygosity a single merged pool at frequency $\bar p$
would produce under random mating. The second is what keeping the pools apart
adds on top of it. Average both over loci with $d_k \equiv 1$, so that the
weighting does not obscure the algebra, and they are exactly the $GD_T$ and
$GD_{BS}$ of the partition of @caballero2002 that @sec-subdivided derived and
`gd_partition()` computes (@tbl-het-partition-identity):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-partition-identity
#| tbl-cap: "Expected heterosis per locus under flat dominance ($d_k \\equiv 1$), split into its shared and divergence terms by `heterosis_partition()` (@eq-het-split), beside $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ of `gd_partition()` on the full A x B factorial of the book's teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers). Residual: absolute difference between the two columns."
hp <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, rep(1, ctx$m)) / ctx$m
gp <- gd_partition(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(hp[["shared"]],     gp[["GD_T"]],  tolerance = 1e-12)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(hp[["divergence"]], gp[["GD_BS"]], tolerance = 1e-12)))
fmt(data.frame(term       = c("shared", "divergence"),
               heterosis  = c(hp[["shared"]], hp[["divergence"]]),
               partition  = c(gp[["GD_T"]],   gp[["GD_BS"]]),
               residual   = c(abs(hp[["shared"]]     - gp[["GD_T"]]),
                              abs(hp[["divergence"]] - gp[["GD_BS"]]))), 12)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The divergence term and $GD_{BS}$

The divergence term, $\sum_k d_k\,y_k^2/2$, **is** the divergence half of expected
heterosis, and with flat dominance ($d_k \equiv 1$), inbred parents and the
complete factorial it is $GD_{BS}$ itself. Under those conditions "between-pool
divergence is the heterosis engine" is an identity, not a slogan; with a $d_k$
that varies across loci $GD_{BS}$ is its unweighted version and the identity
holds for the weighted term only.
:::

One thing to be clear about before reading on. $GD_T$ is the gene diversity of
the *merged* population, and by @sec-subdivided it already contains $GD_{BS}$:
with inbred lines, $GD_T = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}$. Expected F1 heterozygosity is
therefore $GD_{BI} + 2\,GD_{BS}$, the between-pool component counted twice --
once inside the shared term, once as the divergence term. That factor of two is
where the classical result sits. The heterosis of a cross between two
*random-mating* populations is $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ [@falconer1996, Ch. 14],
exactly twice the divergence term of @eq-het-split. The two do not
conflict; they use different mid-parents. Theirs is two random-mating
populations, each carrying its own within-pool heterozygosity, so their $H$ is
the total above $\sum_k d_k (p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk})$. Ours is two inbred
lines carrying none, so the whole F1 heterozygosity is heterosis, and the shared
term is the mean of the two pools' random-mating heterozygosities plus the half
of $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ that $GD_T$ already holds.

That paragraph is an algebraic claim and it can be checked rather than asserted.
Subtract the random-mating mid-parent from the F1's total dominance value and
what is left is $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$, exactly twice this chapter's divergence term (@tbl-het-falconer-ch14):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-falconer-ch14
#| tbl-cap: "Total dominance value of an F1 between two inbred lines (`heterosis_partition()$total`), its random-mating mid-parent $\\sum_k d_k (p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk})$, their difference, and twice the divergence term beside $\\sum_k d_k y_k^2$, for the chapter's pool pair and $d$ (seed 4); sums over loci, in units of $d$."

hpd  <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d)
mid_random_mating <- sum(d * (pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating,
                           2 * hpd[["divergence"]])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(2 * hpd[["divergence"]], sum(d * (pA - pB)^2))))
kv(c(F1_total          = hpd[["total"]],
     mid_random_mating = mid_random_mating,
     difference        = hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating,
     twice_divergence  = 2 * hpd[["divergence"]],
     sum_d_y2          = sum(d * (pA - pB)^2)), 3)
```

The first number is what an F1 between two inbred lines gains over *its* mid-parent
of zero; the third is what the same F1 gains over a mid-parent of two random-mating
pools. They differ by `r fmt(mid_random_mating, 1)` units of dominance value that
the random-mating parents already carry themselves. Which mid-parent is the right
one is not a matter of convention: it is whichever one the programme actually
plants. @sec-heterosis-step1 measures the consequence of getting it wrong.

### A third form: one minus the between-pool coancestry

The sum of the two components has a name of its own. $\theta_{AB} = \mathbf{w}_A'
\mathbf{f}^L \mathbf{w}_B$ is the between-pool coancestry, written $f_{AB}$ in
@sec-subdivided and $\theta_{AB}$ in @sec-catalogue (later), and $\bar f^{L}_{AB}$ in
@sec-coancestry, where its complement is the heterozygous fraction of the F1s: on
the full factorial, where the line weights are uniform, it is the probability
that an allele drawn from a pool-A line and an allele drawn from a pool-B line
are identical in state. Its complement is the whole bracket (checked on the book's data in @tbl-het-theta-ab):

$$GD_T + GD_{BS} \;=\; 1 - \theta_{AB}$$ {#eq-het-theta-ab}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-theta-ab
#| tbl-cap: "$GD_T + GD_{BS}$ from `gd_partition()` beside $1 - \\theta_{AB}$ from `theta_pools()` (@eq-het-theta-ab), on the full A x B factorial of the book's teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers)."
tp <- theta_pools(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]], 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]],
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
kv(c(shared_plus_divergence = gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]],
     one_minus_theta_AB     = 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]]), 8)
```

This one is algebra rather than simulation. `gd_partition()` defines
$GD_T = 1 - \bar f$ and $GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f$ with
$\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} + \theta_B)/4$ and
$\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2$, and the sum collapses to $1 - \theta_{AB}$.
Which is the shortest statement the chapter has to make: **expected F1
heterozygosity is one minus between-pool coancestry.** Everything else here is a
weighting of that quantity, or a way of splitting it. The same identity is
stated numerically for the book's data in @sec-hp-popgen, appears as the diagonal of
the coancestry matrix in @sec-coancestry (@tbl-diagonal) and as the heterosis row
of @tbl-keystone; this section is where it is derived.

## A second identity, at the hybrid level {#sec-heterosis-hybrid-identity}

@sec-subdivided reports `GD_WI_hyb` (@tbl-keystone-check), the within-individual
gene diversity actually carried by the F1s, separately from the line-level partition, because with inbred
parents `GD_WI` is zero by construction and carries no signal. A hybrid's
self-coancestry is $1 - h_i/2$, with $h_i$ its heterozygous fraction, so
`GD_WI_hyb` is half the mean F1 heterozygosity, that is, half the observed heterozygosity $H_o$ of the F1s in @sec-hybrid-programme, and the two levels are linked by @eq-het-wi-hyb, checked in @tbl-het-wi-hyb:

$$2 \cdot GD_{WI\text{-}hyb} = GD_T + GD_{BS}$$ {#eq-het-wi-hyb}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-wi-hyb
#| tbl-cap: "Both sides of @eq-het-wi-hyb on the full A x B factorial (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), and the line-level $GD_{WI}$, which is zero with inbred parents."
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]],
                           tolerance = 1e-12)),
          abs(gp[["GD_WI"]]) < 1e-12)
kv(c(lhs = 2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], rhs = gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]],
     GD_WI = gp[["GD_WI"]]), sig = TRUE)
```

Exact on the full factorial, because every $A \times B$ pairing is present exactly
once. On a *selected* subset it holds only approximately. There $GD_T$ and
$GD_{BS}$ are computed from the line-usage weights, which is what a random
re-pairing of the selected parents would give, while `GD_WI_hyb` scores the pairs
actually chosen. The gap is the pairing structure of the subset.
`tests/testthat/test-dominance.R` asserts the identity to `1e-12` on the full
factorial and, on a *random* 40-hybrid subset at one scale (12 lines per pool,
800 markers; `tests/testthat/setup.R`), bounds the gap with
`expect_equal(tolerance = 5e-3)` (`test-dominance.R`). That
tolerance is **relative**, not absolute: on a gene-diversity value of order 0.4
the absolute bound it enforces is of order `2e-3`. A subset chosen by an optimiser, which concentrates line
usage deliberately, is not covered by that bound. @sec-era-fhom, in the Metrics
and prediction part, measures the gap on four 60-hybrid selections at this book's
scale, of which three are distinct -- one random draw, one max-diversity greedy
and truncation on the index (the index-weighted greedy returns the truncation
set) -- none of them an optimiser's output, and reports the largest departure of
the four.

## Inbreeding depression, and why it does not price $\alpha$ {#sec-heterosis-id}

The same model run backwards gives inbreeding depression ($ID$). A locus at frequency
$p$ in a population with inbreeding coefficient $F$ is heterozygous with
probability $2pq(1-F)$, so the mean declines linearly in $F$
[@falconer1996, Ch. 14]:

$$ID \;=\; 2F\sum_k d_k \, p_k q_k$$ {#eq-het-id}

At $F = 1$ that is exactly the *shared* term of `heterosis_partition()` evaluated
at $p_A = p_B = p$. So the depression of a pool driven to complete homozygosity
and the expected heterosis of a cross made *within* that same pool are one
quantity seen from two sides. @mackay2020 treat heterosis and inbreeding
depression together on that basis, alongside transgressive segregation, which
this chapter does not take up. The identity needs no new machinery (@tbl-het-id-identity):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-id-identity
#| tbl-cap: "Inbreeding depression at $F = 1$ (`inbreeding_depression()`, @eq-het-id) beside the shared term of `heterosis_partition()` at $p_A = p_B$ (pool A of the chapter), and their absolute difference; sums over loci, in units of $d$."
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(inbreeding_depression(pA, d),
                           heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]],
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
kv(c(inbreeding_depression = inbreeding_depression(pA, d),
     shared_term           = heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]],
     deviation             = abs(inbreeding_depression(pA, d) -
                                   heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]])), sig = TRUE)
```

The closed form is checked against simulated genotypes rather than against its
own algebra, which is what `ref_inbreeding_depression()` exists for: it draws
each genotype as identical by descent with probability $F$ and as two independent
alleles otherwise, so the two should agree to Monte Carlo error. @tbl-het-id-mc gives
the closed form, the mean of the eight simulated runs with different seeds, the
standard deviation of one run, and the standardised difference $z$:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-id-mc
#| tbl-cap: "Closed-form inbreeding depression at $F = 0.6$ on the first 300 loci of pool A (@eq-het-id) against `ref_inbreeding_depression()`: mean of 8 simulated runs of 20000 genotypes each (seeds 1 to 8), standard deviation of one run, and $z$, the difference of the mean from the closed form in standard errors of the mean (s.d. of the runs over $\\sqrt{8}$); sums over loci, in units of $d$ (`z` is dimensionless)."
k <- seq_len(300)
n_id <- 8
id_sim <- vapply(seq_len(n_id), function(s)
  ref_inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6, n = 20000, seed = s), numeric(1))
id_closed <- inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6)
id_se <- sd(id_sim) / sqrt(n_id)
kv(c(closed_form = id_closed, simulated_mean = mean(id_sim), mc_sd_one_run = sd(id_sim),
     z = (mean(id_sim) - id_closed) / id_se), 3)
```

Result. The standard deviation of one simulated run over the `r n_id` seeds is
`r fmt(sd(id_sim), 3)`; the mean of the `r n_id` runs differs from the closed form by
`r fmt(mean(id_sim) - inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6), 3)`, which is
`r fmt((mean(id_sim) - inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6)) / (sd(id_sim) / sqrt(n_id)), 1)`
standard errors of that mean. The closed form and the simulation agree within the
Monte Carlo error of this run (300 loci of one pool, $F = 0.6$).

Now the part that matters, because the obvious next step is wrong.

It is tempting to argue: $\alpha$ budgets a loss of gene diversity; with inbred
parents the quantity it budgets is $GD_T = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}$ of the merged
candidate set, the mean over loci of $2\bar p_k\bar q_k$ (@tbl-keystone), and
not $GD_{BI}$ alone; inbreeding depression is $2F\sum_k d_k\,p_kq_k$; therefore
spending $\alpha$ costs yield in the current cycle, and *that* is the price of the
budget. The algebra does not support it (@tbl-het-inbred-zero).


```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-inbred-zero
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute dominance contribution, `heterosis_value()`, of any pool-A line of the book's teaching scale (coded 0/1), in units of $d$."
stopifnot(max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d))) == 0)
kv(c(max_dominance_contribution_of_an_inbred_line = max(abs(heterosis_value(U, d)))))
```

Zero, exactly. A fully inbred line has no heterozygous loci, so its dominance
contribution is zero **whatever the pool's allele frequencies are**. (On the
simulated lines, coded 0/1, this holds for any matrix: no entry can equal 0.5, so
the check illustrates the algebra and tests nothing about the pool; it is
informative only on real genotypes, where the matrix can carry 0.5.) In a
programme whose parents are inbred lines the depression was paid in full when the
lines were made; it is a constant, and it does not move when the pool
subsequently loses diversity. @eq-het-id describes the gap between a
hypothetical random-mating pool and its inbred derivatives, and that gap
*shrinks* as $p_kq_k$ shrinks -- but nothing in the programme stands at the
random-mating end of it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Inbreeding depression is not the current-cycle price of the diversity budget

This is the same fact that makes $GD_{WI}$ exactly zero in the partition of
@sec-subdivided (@tbl-keystone), and it has the same cause: with inbred parents
there is no within-individual variation left to lose. Two consequences.

The cost of $\alpha$ in this system is not a yield loss booked this season. Whether
it is paid later, as lost response, is a different question. @sec-response-genic
states the condition under which gene diversity stands in for genic variance --
only through $GD_{WS}$, which is not what $\alpha$ budgets, and only if effect
sizes are unrelated to which loci lose diversity -- and does not test it; this
chapter does not either, and so does not say that the cost of $\alpha$ arrives in
the additive variance. @sec-cycles runs selection under the budget on an additive
index.

And inbreeding depression **is** the live quantity wherever the population is
only partially inbred ($0 < F < 1$: the F2, F3 and F4 generations that
@sec-sizing sizes, where $F$ is still climbing). **This book does not model it
there.** @sec-sizing lists phenotypic inbreeding depression among what it does not
model (its SA9), and the only place the book applies the quantity to a population is at $F = 1$
(@sec-alphasimr), where it is the shared term above. The one other evaluation, at
$F = 0.6$ in @tbl-het-id-mc, checks the formula against simulation on 300 loci of one
pool and is not a partially inbred generation of the programme. @eq-het-id gives the
expected depression at inbreeding coefficient $F$ relative to random mating;
@sec-genomic-era writes the same formula for the crossing block without computing
it, and the book computes it for no partially inbred generation.
:::

Note also what this does *not* say. Expected heterosis in the product is a
separate question. @sec-heterosis-flat answers it for the neutral case: under
drift the shared term lost and the divergence term gained cancel in expectation
(@eq-het-bn-halves), so expected hybrid heterosis is invariant for a $d$ drawn
independently of the frequencies. Under selection the frequencies move
directionally, and what happens to expected heterosis is then the alignment
question of @sec-heterosis-alignment, which can go either way. In neither case is
the diversity loss itself an immediate dominance cost. Whether it is a cost later,
in the variance available to select on, is the conditional question of
@sec-response-genic, not a result of this chapter.

## When genetic distance predicts heterosis exactly {#sec-heterosis-distance}

Before the corrections start, one special case is worth having, because it is the
only case in which marker distance and heterosis are the same number.

Set $d_k \equiv d$, constant across loci. Then $H$ stops being a weighted count and
becomes a plain one: $d$ times the number of loci at which the two parents differ.
For inbred lines that count is exactly what the coancestry kernel of
@sec-coancestry measures, so for a cross between pool-A line $i$ and pool-B line $j$

$$H_{ij} \;=\; d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij}) \;=\; d\,m\,\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}^2$$ {#eq-het-distance}

where $\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}$ is the modified Rogers distance between the two lines.
@tbl-het-distance checks both equalities on the full factorial.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-distance
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute difference over the full A x B factorial between the heterosis under flat dominance ($d_k \\equiv 1$) and $m(1 - f^L_{ij})$, and between it and $m\\,\\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}^2$ (@eq-het-distance), in units of $d$."
h1 <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, rep(1, ctx$m))
fL <- molecular_coancestry(L / 2)
ab <- cbind(ctx$ped$a, ctx$ped$b)
stopifnot(max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * (1 - fL[ab]))) < 1e-9,
          max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * mrd_matrix(L / 2)[ab]^2)) < 1e-9)
kv(c(vs_coancestry = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * (1 - fL[ab]))),
     vs_mrd        = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * mrd_matrix(L / 2)[ab]^2))), sig = TRUE)
```

Both residuals are at machine precision. Under flat dominance, heterosis and
molecular coancestry are one statistic seen twice -- the identity of the modified
Rogers distance with coancestry is Trap 1 of @sec-stages, met later; the link to
heterosis is made here -- and the diversity kernel this whole book runs on turns out
to be the right object for the heterosis question as well.

Flat $d$ is also precisely the condition under which $H$ is a function of marker
distance alone. It is a strong condition, and it fails as soon as $d$ varies: two
crosses at the same distance then differ by *which* loci they differ at. With the
gamma-distributed dominance effects used everywhere else in this chapter the relationship
survives but stops being an identity (@tbl-het-cor-d):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-cor-d
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation over the 625 crosses of the full factorial between heterosis and $1 - f^L_{ij}$, under flat dominance (`cor_uniform_d`) and under the gamma-distributed $d$ of the chapter (`cor_real_d`; shape 2, rate 4, seed 4). Dimensionless."
kv(c(cor_uniform_d = cor(h1, 1 - fL[ab]),
     cor_real_d    = cor(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d), 1 - fL[ab])), 3)
```

A correlation of `r round(cor(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d), 1 - fL[ab]), 2)` is a
useful predictor and a poor identity. Two things move it, and both are properties
of the germplasm rather than of the statistic: how $d$ is spread over the loci at
which the parents differ, which is what @sec-heterosis-alignment is about, and --
once the premise that the marker panel is the set of dominance loci (@sec-heterosis-premises) is relaxed -- how well the panel tags the causal loci.
Under flat $d$ on a panel that *is* the causal set the correlation is 1 by
@eq-het-distance. Departing from either condition generally lowers it -- not
always, since a $d$ that varies only across loci at which no pair of parents
differs changes no $H_i$ at all -- and by how much is something this chapter does
not attempt to predict.

## Divergence is not a bonus {#sec-heterosis-flat}

Read `divergence` as free money and you will reach for $F_{ST}$. Do not.

Draw the pools further apart and watch all three terms (@tbl-het-sweep). Nothing
here is selected. The claim to be tested is an expectation (@eq-het-bn-total,
@eq-het-bn-halves); the sweep has one draw per row, so it can show that the
totals stay close to the expected level and that the two changes are of the same
size, not that they are equal.
Each point re-draws both pools from the *same* ancestral frequencies -- the
ancestral vector is fixed by `seed = 5` and shared across the sweep, while the two
pool-frequency vectors are fresh Balding-Nichols draws [@balding1995] at each `fst`
(@sec-notation) -- so what varies along the sweep is how far the draw scatters
and nothing else.

Two quantities are kept apart in this chapter, each with its own symbol
(@sec-hp-inbreeding, @sec-notation). $F_{BN}$ is the Balding-Nichols parameter of
the simulation, `fst` in the code: the variance of a pool's allele frequency
around the ancestral one $p^{*}$ (@eq-balding-nichols, stated later, in @sec-simulating-crosses; a quantity of the draw, never observed; $q^{*} = 1 - p^{*}$), in units of $p^{*}(1-p^{*})$. Every expectation below is a
function of $F_{BN}$. $F_{ST}$ is the statistic $GD_{BS}/GD_T$ computed on the
pools' frequencies [@caballero2002, Eq. 8], which under Balding-Nichols
estimates approximately $F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})$ rather than $F_{BN}$
(@sec-notation) and is larger again on finite pools. Where the text says that
$F_{ST}$ "is a function of the frequencies only" (@sec-heterosis-alignment,
@sec-heterosis-step8) it means the statistic. No conclusion here depends on the
difference between the two: both are functions of the frequencies, and $d$ enters
neither.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-sweep
#| tbl-cap: "Neutral divergence sweep. For each target `fst` (the Balding-Nichols parameter), both pools are redrawn from one fixed ancestral frequency vector (seed 5) at the book's teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers); one draw per row, no replication. Shared, divergence and total: expected heterosis per locus at $d_k \\equiv 1$ (@eq-het-split). Last three columns: the complementarity statistics of `pool_complementarity()`."
sweep_het <- function(fst) {
  cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = 5))
  Lf <- simulate_lines(cf)
  pl <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B))
  Pf <- pool_freqs(Lf / 2, pl)
  hp <- heterosis_partition(Pf["A", ], Pf["B", ], rep(1, cf$m)) / cf$m
  cm <- pool_complementarity(Lf / 2, pl)
  data.frame(fst = fst, shared = hp[["shared"]], divergence = hp[["divergence"]],
             total = hp[["total"]],
             frac_opposite_fixed = cm[["frac_opposite_fixed"]],
             mean_abs_delta_p = cm[["mean_abs_delta_p"]],
             mean_sq_delta_p = cm[["mean_sq_delta_p"]])
}
sw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45), sweep_het))
# Read again in @sec-heterosis-step5: no marker is fixed for opposite alleles
# at any grid point up to fst = 0.10, while the divergence term has already
# more than doubled between fst = 0.02 and 0.10.
stopifnot(all(sw$frac_opposite_fixed[sw$fst <= 0.10] == 0))
fmt(sw, 4)
```

Across the sweep the divergence term rises by a factor of
`r round(max(sw$divergence)/min(sw$divergence), 1)`. The comparison that matters
is in absolute units, not in ratios: divergence gains
`r round(sw$divergence[nrow(sw)] - sw$divergence[1], 4)` per locus and the shared
term loses `r round(sw$shared[1] - sw$shared[nrow(sw)], 4)`. The two changes are
not equal in this draw, because each row is one sample of both pools; the
expectation says they are equal, and the sweep shows them within
`r round(100 * abs((sw$divergence[nrow(sw)] - sw$divergence[1]) / (sw$shared[1] - sw$shared[nrow(sw)]) - 1), 0)` %
of each other, with no replicate to say how far apart two draws can be. The total
does not move in expectation, and in this draw the six totals lie between
`r round(min(sw$total), 4)` and `r round(max(sw$total), 4)` (the `total` column of
@tbl-het-sweep).

### The two terms, term by term

The algebra is one line. Pool A and pool B are drawn *independently* around a
common ancestral frequency $p^{*}$, so $\mathbb{E}[p_A] = \mathbb{E}[p_B] = p^{*}$ and
$\mathbb{E}[p_A p_B] = p^{*2}$. Therefore

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B\right] = 2p^{*}(1-p^{*}),$$ {#eq-het-bn-total}

which contains no $F_{BN}$ at all. With ancestral frequencies drawn uniformly on
$[0.05, 0.95]$ the predicted level is $\mathbb{E}[2p^{*}(1-p^{*})] =$ `r round(2*(0.5 - (0.9^2/12 + 0.25)), 4)`,
against a simulated mean of `r round(mean(sw$total), 4)` across the whole sweep
(the six rows range from `r round(min(sw$total), 4)` to `r round(max(sw$total), 4)`).

That the *sum* is flat is the headline, but the Balding-Nichols model predicts
each half separately, which is the sharper statement. Under it
$\mathrm{Var}(p_A) = \mathrm{Var}(p_B) = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$, so
$\mathrm{Var}(\bar p) = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})/2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(y) = 2F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$.
Substituting:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\right] = 2p^{*}(1-p^{*})\left(1 - \tfrac{F_{BN}}{2}\right),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\!\left[y^2/2\right] = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$$ {#eq-het-bn-halves}

The shared term loses $F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$ and the divergence term gains
$F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$ in expectation over the draw of the pools: the same expression with
opposite signs, exactly and at every value of $F_{BN}$, not approximately. Both predictions are parameter-free once the
ancestral distribution is fixed, so they can be laid straight on top of the sweep (@tbl-het-sweep-bn,
@fig-heterosis-sweep):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-sweep-bn
#| tbl-cap: "Measured shared and divergence terms of @tbl-het-sweep (per locus, $d_k \\equiv 1$) beside their Balding-Nichols predictions (@eq-het-bn-halves), computed with no fitted parameter from $E[2p^{*}(1-p^{*})]$ for ancestral $p^{*}$ uniform on [0.05, 0.95]."
Ep <- 2 * (0.5 - (0.9^2 / 12 + 0.25))      # E[2p*(1-p*)] for p* ~ U(0.05, 0.95)
sw$pred_shared     <- Ep * (1 - sw$fst / 2)
sw$pred_divergence <- Ep * sw$fst / 2
fmt(sw[, c("fst", "shared", "pred_shared", "divergence", "pred_divergence")], 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heterosis-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Expected heterosis per locus at $d_k \\equiv 1$ (total, black filled circles) and its shared (grey triangles) and divergence (black open squares) components (@eq-het-split) as the pools are driven apart by drift alone, against the target Balding-Nichols `fst` ($F_{BN}$). Each point is one draw of both pools from one fixed ancestral frequency vector (seed 5) at the book's teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), with no replication. Dashed lines are the Balding-Nichols predictions for the shared (grey) and divergence (black) components separately (@eq-het-bn-halves), with no fitted parameter; the dotted line is the mean total over the sweep. Nothing is selected."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of expected heterosis per locus against target fst from 0.02 to 0.45. The divergence component rises from near zero, the shared component falls by nearly the same amount (the two changes differ by a few per cent in this draw), and their total stays nearly flat; dashed lines show the Balding-Nichols prediction for each component and a dotted line the mean total."
plot(sw$fst, sw$total, type = "b", pch = 19, col = book_pal[["ink"]], ylim = c(0, 0.40),
     xaxt = "n",
     xlab = expression("target " * F[BN] * " between pools"),
     ylab = expression("expected heterosis per locus (units of " * d * ", " * d[k] == 1 * ")"))
lines(sw$fst, sw$shared, type = "b", pch = 17, col = book_pal[["mid"]])
lines(sw$fst, sw$divergence, type = "b", pch = 0, col = book_pal[["ink"]])
lines(sw$fst, sw$pred_shared, lty = 2, col = book_pal[["mid"]])
lines(sw$fst, sw$pred_divergence, lty = 2, col = book_pal[["ink"]])
abline(h = mean(sw$total), lty = 3, col = book_pal[["ink"]])
axis(1, at = sw$fst, labels = sprintf("%.2f", sw$fst), cex.axis = 0.85)  # every grid point
legend("right", c("total", "shared", "divergence", "Balding-Nichols, shared",
                  "Balding-Nichols, divergence", "mean total"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       pch = c(19, 17, 0, NA, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 2, 2, 3),
       col = book_pal[c("ink", "mid", "ink", "mid", "ink", "ink")])
grid()
```

The measured divergence sits above its prediction at every `fst`, and the measured
shared term about the same distance below it. That is not drift, it is
estimation. The
pool frequencies are estimated from `r book_cfg$n_pool_A` and
`r book_cfg$n_pool_B` sampled lines, and a frequency estimated from $n$ lines
carries sampling variance $\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) = pq/n$. Conditional on the true pool frequencies,
$\mathbb{E}[\hat y^2/2] = y^2/2 + [\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_A) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_B)]/2$ and
$\mathbb{E}[2\hat{\bar p}(1 - \hat{\bar p})] = 2\bar p(1 - \bar p) - [\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_A) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_B)]/2$:
equal and opposite, so the total estimated from sample frequencies is unbiased
while each half is not.

The offset is not constant along the sweep. It is proportional to
$\mathbb{E}[p_Aq_A + p_Bq_B]$, which the pools themselves erode as they diverge,
so it shrinks with $(1 - F_{BN})$: about
`r round(Ep * (1 - sw$fst[1]) * (1 / book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1 / book_cfg$n_pool_B) / 4, 4)`
per locus at `fst =` `r sw$fst[1]`, down to
`r round(Ep * (1 - sw$fst[nrow(sw)]) * (1 / book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1 / book_cfg$n_pool_B) / 4, 4)`
at `fst =` `r sw$fst[nrow(sw)]`, against measured gaps of
`r round(sw$divergence[1] - sw$pred_divergence[1], 4)` and
`r round(sw$divergence[nrow(sw)] - sw$pred_divergence[nrow(sw)], 4)`.

Those two pairs do not agree equally well. At `fst =` `r sw$fst[1]` prediction
and measurement are within
`r round(100 * abs((sw$divergence[1] - sw$pred_divergence[1]) / (Ep * (1 - sw$fst[1]) * (1 / book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1 / book_cfg$n_pool_B) / 4) - 1))` %
of each other; at `fst =` `r sw$fst[nrow(sw)]` the measured gap is
`r round(100 * (1 - (sw$divergence[nrow(sw)] - sw$pred_divergence[nrow(sw)]) / (Ep * (1 - sw$fst[nrow(sw)]) * (1 / book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1 / book_cfg$n_pool_B) / 4)))` %
*below* the predicted offset. The formula gives an expectation; each row of the
sweep is one draw of `r book_cfg$m` loci at one seed, and the scatter of that
draw is not constant either. $\mathrm{Var}(y)$ is $2F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$, so the
per-locus divergence $y^2/2$ has a variance that grows with $F_{BN}$ while the
number of loci averaging it stays fixed -- the high-`fst` rows are the noisy
ones, and the agreement at the bottom of the sweep is the more informative of the
two. The offset is the right order and the right sign at both ends; it is not a
per-point prediction, and nothing below rests on it being one.

What changes by an order of magnitude along the sweep is not the offset but the
signal it sits on: at `fst = 0.02` the offset exceeds the predicted divergence of
`r round(sw$pred_divergence[1], 4)`, and by `fst = 0.45` it is a small fraction of
it. A pool pair's *apparent* divergence overstates its true divergence, most
severely when the true divergence is small and the pools are few.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Every unit of divergence is paid for out of the shared term, $GD_T$

Under neutral divergence the trade is one for one in expectation.
Drifting the pools apart does not create expected heterosis; it relocates it from the shared term
to the divergence term. A programme that maximises $F_{ST}$ by drift has bought
no expected heterosis and has spent gene diversity to do it.
:::

The term that pays unit for unit is the shared term, $GD_T$, which contains
$GD_{BS}$; it is not the within-pool term $GD_{WS}$ (the $GD_{BI}$ of the budget paragraph
above, since $GD_{WS} = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}$ and $GD_{WI} = 0$ with inbred parents). With inbred parents and the
complete factorial $GD_T = GD_{WS} + GD_{BS}$ per locus (the identity
$2\bar p\bar q = p_Aq_A + p_Bq_B + y^2/2$ of @sec-response-genic), so by
@eq-het-bn-halves $GD_{WS}$ falls by
$F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$ (the shared term's loss) plus the $F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$ that $GD_{BS}$
gains: **twice** what $GD_{BS}$ gains, the accounting of @sec-keystone. Both
statements are expectations over the draw of the pools, under the conditions above,
and the chapter does not measure $GD_{WS}$ along the sweep.
This is the mechanism behind @sec-stages Trap 3, in the Metrics and prediction
part. That section states the symptom
-- "$F_{ST}$ keeps rising as pools drift apart at loci that are *already*
divergent, which buys no additional heterosis" -- and points here for the reason.
@tbl-het-sweep and @fig-heterosis-sweep are that reason.

## What actually buys heterosis {#sec-heterosis-alignment}

If divergence per se is worth nothing, why do heterotic groups work?

Because real pools are not diverged at random with respect to $d$. The divergence
term is $\sum_k d_k y_k^2 / 2$, a *weighted* sum. It grows when the loci that
diverge are the loci that carry dominance; under drift the two are independent,
which is exactly why the total was flat.

### Alignment is a covariance

That sentence can be a number rather than a word. A sum of products is $m$ times
a mean times a mean, plus $m$ times a covariance -- the population covariance
with divisor $m$, which is why the chunk rescales `cov()`:

$$\sum_k d_k\,y_k^2 / 2 \;=\; \frac{m}{2}\Big[\, \bar d \; \overline{y^2}
  \;+\; \mathrm{cov}(d,\, y^2) \,\Big]$$ {#eq-het-alignment}

```{r}
y2 <- (pA - pB)^2
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(d * y2 / 2),
  ctx$m / 2 * (mean(d) * mean(y2) + cov(d, y2) * (ctx$m - 1) / ctx$m))))
c(divergence = sum(d * y2 / 2),
  from_parts = ctx$m / 2 * (mean(d) * mean(y2) + cov(d, y2) * (ctx$m - 1) / ctx$m))
```

The first bracketed term is what $F_{ST}$ can see: average divergence times
average dominance. The second is what it cannot. **Alignment is
$\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$**, and no statistic computed from allele frequencies alone
can contain it, because $d$ does not appear in one.

### The scenarios

Hold the pools fixed, hold $F_{ST}$ fixed, hold the multiset of dominance
effects fixed, and change only which locus gets which $d_k$. `aligned` gives
the largest $d_k$ to the largest $y_k^2$, `anti-aligned` does the reverse, and
`independent` is the draw as made (@tbl-het-alignment, @fig-heterosis-alignment):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-alignment
#| tbl-cap: "Expected heterosis of one pool pair (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers) under three placements of the same dominance effects across loci: largest $d_k$ on largest $y_k^2$ (aligned), the reverse (anti-aligned), and as drawn (independent; $d_k$ gamma with shape 2 and rate 4, seed 4). `cor_d_y2`: correlation between $d$ and $y^2$ over loci. Shared, divergence, total: sums over loci, in units of $d$. Relative: total over the total of the independent placement."
mk <- function(dec) { v <- numeric(ctx$m); v[order(y2)] <- sort(d, decreasing = dec); v }
scen <- list(`anti-aligned` = mk(TRUE), `independent` = d, `aligned` = mk(FALSE))
al <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scen), function(n) {
  h <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, scen[[n]])
  data.frame(scenario = n, cor_d_y2 = cor(scen[[n]], y2),
             shared = h[["shared"]], divergence = h[["divergence"]], total = h[["total"]])
}))
al$relative <- al$total / al$total[al$scenario == "independent"]
fmt(al, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heterosis-alignment
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("Expected heterosis of one pool pair (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers) under three placements of the same dominance effects across loci (@tbl-het-alignment), as stacked shared (grey) and divergence (black) terms, summed over loci in units of $d$; the label above each bar is its total relative to the independent placement. The same two pools, the same $F_{ST}$, and the same set of dominance effects in all three bars -- only their placement across loci differs. Expected heterosis moves by a factor of %.2f between the extremes. $F_{ST}$ cannot see any of this, because $d$ does not enter it.", max(al$total) / min(al$total))
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart with three bars, anti-aligned, independent and aligned, each split into a shared and a divergence part of expected heterosis. The bars rise from anti-aligned to aligned, and each is labelled with its total relative to the independent bar."
bars <- function(col, ...) barplot(rbind(al$shared, al$divergence), beside = FALSE,
                                   col = col, border = NA, ...)
bars(NA, names.arg = al$scenario, ylab = expression("expected heterosis (units of " * d * ", summed over loci)"),
     xlab = "placement of the dominance effects across loci")
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL)                        # grid first, bars and labels over it
bp <- bars(book_pal[c("mid", "ink")], add = TRUE, axes = FALSE, names.arg = rep("", nrow(al)))
legend("topleft", c("shared", "divergence"), fill = book_pal[c("mid", "ink")],
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8, border = NA)
lab <- sprintf("%.2fx", al$relative)
y0  <- al$total + 0.015 * diff(par("usr")[3:4])
rect(bp - strwidth(lab, cex = 0.8) / 2 - 0.03, y0 - 0.3 * strheight(lab, cex = 0.8),
     bp + strwidth(lab, cex = 0.8) / 2 + 0.03, y0 + 1.3 * strheight(lab, cex = 0.8),
     col = "white", border = NA)                # halo: no grid line through a label
text(bp, y0, lab, adj = c(0.5, 0), cex = 0.8, xpd = NA)
```

$F_{ST}$ is identical in all three rows of @tbl-het-alignment and in all three bars of
@fig-heterosis-alignment -- it is a function of the frequencies only, and $d$
never enters it. Expected heterosis ranges over a factor of
`r round(max(al$total)/min(al$total), 2)` in this generating model (one pool pair
and one gamma draw of $d$, not varied).

### Isolating the divergence channel

One honest qualification. Sorting $d$ against $y^2$ moves the *shared* term as
well, because $y^2$ is not independent of $2\bar p(1 - \bar p)$: a locus with a
large frequency difference tends to sit at an intermediate mean frequency. Part
of the effect above therefore arrives through the shared half, not the divergence
half.

The channel can be separated. Permute $d$ only *within* groups of loci that share
a value of the shared weight $2\bar p(1 - \bar p)$. The shared term is then
invariant by construction -- exactly, not approximately -- and whatever moves is
the divergence channel alone (@tbl-het-alignment-stratified):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-alignment-stratified
#| tbl-cap: "The aligned and anti-aligned placements of @tbl-het-alignment repeated with $d$ permuted only within groups of loci sharing the same shared weight $2\\bar p(1 - \\bar p)$, so the shared term is identical in both rows by construction. Sums over loci, in units of $d$."
hz  <- 2 * ((pA + pB) / 2) * (1 - (pA + pB) / 2)
grp <- split(seq_len(ctx$m), round(hz, 9))
strat <- function(dec) {
  v <- numeric(ctx$m)
  for (i in grp) v[i[order(y2[i])]] <- sort(d[i], decreasing = dec)
  v
}
st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(aligned = FALSE, `anti-aligned` = TRUE), function(dec)
  as.data.frame(as.list(heterosis_partition(pA, pB, strat(dec))))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(st$shared[1], st$shared[2])))
fmt(st, 4)
```

The groups are the distinct values of the shared weight: there are
`r length(grp)` of them, because pool frequencies computed from
`r book_cfg$n_pool_A` lines are multiples of $1/$`r book_cfg$n_pool_A`, so $\bar p$
takes at most `r 2 * book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1` values and $2\bar p(1 - \bar p)$, which is
symmetric about $\bar p = 1/2$, at most `r book_cfg$n_pool_A + 1`; with continuous
frequencies every locus would be its own group and the construction would return $d$
unchanged. The shared column is identical to the digit; the divergence term still moves by
a factor of `r round(st$divergence[1] / st$divergence[2], 1)` and the total by
`r round(100 * (st$total[1] / st$total[2] - 1))` %. The alignment result survives
its own control.

## Reading the S1 panel

@sec-stages will log `frac_opposite_fixed` and `mean_abs_delta_p` every cycle as
stand-ins for heterosis potential. The sweep of @sec-heterosis-flat says how good they are.

`mean_sq_delta_p` is not a proxy at all. It is $\overline{y^2}$, so half of it is
the unweighted divergence term $GD_{BS}$, exactly (@tbl-het-msdp):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-msdp
#| tbl-cap: "Half the mean of `mean_sq_delta_p` and the mean divergence term over the six rows of @tbl-het-sweep, per locus at $d_k \\equiv 1$; the two agree row by row."
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sw$mean_sq_delta_p / 2, sw$divergence)))
kv(c(half_mean_sq = mean(sw$mean_sq_delta_p) / 2,
     divergence   = mean(sw$divergence)), 6)
```

What it cannot carry is the weighting by $d$, which is the point of
@sec-heterosis-alignment; the frequency half of the divergence term it reports without loss.

`frac_opposite_fixed` is a different matter (its column in @tbl-het-sweep).

Up to `fst = 0.10` it is exactly zero -- not one marker in `r book_cfg$m`
qualifies -- and it first exceeds 1 % of markers at
`fst` = `r sw$fst[which(sw$frac_opposite_fixed > 0.01)[1]]`, near the top of
the sweep. It counts *near-fixed* opposite loci, and the divergence lives at
intermediate frequency differences, which the threshold discards.

**Log `mean_sq_delta_p`.** It is exact, it is monotone across the whole sweep,
and it costs one squaring more than the statistic already being logged.
`pool_complementarity()` and `s1_monitor()` return it.

## General and specific combining ability {#sec-heterosis-gca-sca}

Everything so far has been about $\mathbb{E}[H]$. Now the spread.

The same expansion that produced the shared/divergence split produces the
combining-ability decomposition, with no new machinery and no model fitting. Let
$u_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}$ be the genotype of pool-A line $i$ at locus $k$ and
$v_{jk}$ that of pool-B line $j$, and write each as its pool frequency plus a
deviation, $u = p_A + \delta u$ and $v = p_B + \delta v$. The per-locus
heterozygosity of the cross, $u + v - 2uv$, expands to

$$u + v - 2uv \;=\; \underbrace{p_A + p_B - 2p_Ap_B}_{\text{mean}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_B)\,\delta u}_{\text{parent A}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v}_{\text{parent B}}
  \;-\; \underbrace{2\,\delta u\, \delta v}_{\text{both}}$$ {#eq-het-expansion}

Four terms: one constant, one linear in each parent, one bilinear. Weight by $d_k$,
sum over loci, and a decomposition of the form of the classical one into general
and specific combining ability [@sprague1942; @griffing1956] falls out,

$$H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}$$ {#eq-het-gca-sca}

with

$$g^A_i = \sum_k d_k (1 - 2p_{Bk})\,\delta u_{ik}, \qquad
  s_{ij} = -2 \sum_k d_k\, \delta u_{ik}\, \delta v_{jk}$$ {#eq-het-gca-sca-terms}

and $g^B_j$ symmetrically.

**What these symbols denote.** $\mu$, $g^A_i$, $g^B_j$ and $s_{ij}$ are used here
for the decomposition of the mid-parent heterosis $H_{ij}$ (@eq-het-value), not of
the cross mean $\bar y_{ij}$ of @eq-hp-gca-sca (the model for a factorial between
two sets of lines, the North Carolina Design II of @comstock1948, as in
@sec-hybrid-programme). For the cross mean, with additive
effects $a_k$ and no epistasis, the GCA of pool-A line $i$ is
$\sum_k [a_k + d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})]\,\delta u_{ik}$ (@sec-mating-estimation). The
$g^A_i$ of @eq-het-gca-sca-terms is the **dominance part** of that GCA, with the
additive part $\sum_k a_k\,\delta u_{ik}$ -- which cancels from $H_{ij}$ -- removed;
$s_{ij}$ is the same object in both. Where the two have to be told apart, this
book writes **GCA for heterosis** for the term of this section and GCA, unqualified,
for the term of @eq-hp-gca-sca. The exact orthogonal split is the book's own; the
concept of combining ability is that of the sources cited above.

What is linear in one parent is general combining
ability: it is carried into every cross that parent enters. What is bilinear
depends on *which two* lines met, and is specific combining ability. Because the
deviations are taken from each pool's own line frequencies they sum to zero over
that pool's lines, which is what makes the three components mean zero and
mutually orthogonal. `heterosis_gca_sca()` is @eq-het-expansion weighted by $d_k$ and nothing more:

```{r}
cat(deparse(heterosis_gca_sca), sep = "\n")
```

It reconstructs every hybrid in the factorial exactly, and all three components
are mean zero (@tbl-het-gca-sca-check):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-gca-sca-check
#| tbl-cap: "Reconstruction of the heterosis of every hybrid of the full factorial by `heterosis_gca_sca()` (@eq-het-gca-sca): largest absolute residual, $|\\mu - \\bar H|$ (`mu_vs_mean`), and the means of the pool-A GCA and of the SCA components, in units of $d$."
cs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)
H  <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)
ia <- ctx$ped$a
ib <- ctx$ped$b - nA
tol_H <- 1e-9 * max(abs(H))                  # relative to the scale of H
recon_gap <- max(abs(H - (cs$mu + cs$gca_A[ia] + cs$gca_B[ib] + cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)])))
stopifnot(recon_gap < tol_H, abs(cs$mu - mean(H)) < tol_H,
          abs(mean(cs$gca_A)) < tol_H, abs(mean(cs$gca_B)) < tol_H,
          abs(mean(cs$sca)) < tol_H)
kv(c(max_residual = max(abs(H - (cs$mu + cs$gca_A[ia] + cs$gca_B[ib] +
                                 cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)]))),
     mu_vs_mean   = abs(cs$mu - mean(H)),
     mean_gca_A   = mean(cs$gca_A), mean_sca = mean(cs$sca)), sig = TRUE)
```

This is not a decomposition that resembles the two-way analysis of variance. It
*is* the two-way analysis of variance: $\mu$, $g^A$ and $g^B$ are the grand mean
and the row and column effects of the $H_{ij}$ table, and $s_{ij}$ is the
interaction residual of the additive fit, to machine precision (@tbl-het-lm-gap):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-lm-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute difference between the residuals of `lm(H ~ factor(ia) + factor(ib))` and the SCA matrix of `heterosis_gca_sca()`, over the full factorial, in units of $d$."
lm_gap <- max(abs(resid(lm(H ~ factor(ia) + factor(ib))) - cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)]))
stopifnot(lm_gap < tol_H)
kv(c(max_abs_difference = lm_gap), sig = TRUE)

```

Both are asserted: the reconstruction residual is `r fmt_sci(recon_gap)` and the
`lm()` gap `r fmt_sci(lm_gap)`, against a tolerance of `r fmt_sci(tol_H)`
(`1e-9` times the largest $|H_{ij}|$, `r fmt(max(abs(H)), 1)`).

The tester-based schemes of the book (@sec-hp-cycle) evaluate candidates by their
cross performance against a sample of the other pool. @comstock1949 is the
procedure the book cites for them; the paper's title states that it was designed
"to make maximum use of both general and specific combining ability", and this
chapter reports nothing of that paper beyond its title. The algebra above says
what each component is made of, and @sec-heterosis-gca-average works out, as the
book's own derivation, what a tester-based mean of $H$ carries.

### GCA is an average effect in the other pool's background {#sec-heterosis-gca-average}

Look at the weight on $\delta u$: it is $d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})$, and $1 - 2p_B$ is
$q_B - p_B$. That is the frequency factor of the classical average effect of a
gene substitution, $a + d\,(q - p)$ [@falconer1996, Ch. 7], with two differences:
the additive part $a$ is absent, because it belongs to the parental mean and not
to $H$, and the frequencies are **pool B's**, not pool A's.

This is the whole reason combining ability is not a property of a line. A pool-A
line's alleles are always substituted into a pool-B background, so its general
combining ability for heterosis is a dominance effect *evaluated at the tester
pool's frequencies*. Change the tester pool and every number changes. Two limits
follow immediately:

- A locus at which the tester pool sits at $p_B = 0.5$ contributes **exactly
  zero** to $g^A$, whatever $\delta u_{ik}$ is. It still contributes to $g^B$,
  through $(1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v_{jk}$, and to $s_{ij}$; what it cannot do is
  discriminate between pool-A parents.
- A locus at which the tester pool is fixed, $p_B \in \{0, 1\}$, has
  $\delta v \equiv 0$, so it contributes $\pm d_k\,\delta u_{ik}$ to $g^A$ and
  nothing to either $g^B$ or $s_{ij}$. The cross is then predictable from the
  pool-A parent by itself.

Between those two limits sits every real programme, and @sec-heterosis-relocation
is about which limit divergence pushes it towards.

**What a tester-based mean of $H$ carries (the book's own derivation).** The
following is algebra in this chapter's model -- fully inbred candidates (the first premise of @sec-heterosis-premises),
$H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}$ -- and not a report of what any published
scheme does or selects on; whether the procedure of @comstock1949 works on lines or
on heterozygous plants, this chapter does not say, and the decomposition above is
derived for lines only. Evaluate each pool-A candidate by the mean of its $H_{ij}$
over a set $T$ of $k$ pool-B testers. Because the deviations sum to zero over the
pool, that mean is, over **all** $n_B$ testers, exactly $\mu + g^A_i$: $s_{ij}$
averages out and $g^A_i$ is the whole of what distinguishes candidates. Over a
**sample** of $k < n_B$ testers it is $\mu + g^A_i + \bar g^B_T + \bar s_{i\cdot T}$,
where $\bar g^B_T$ is the same for every candidate (it moves the level, not the
ranking) and $\bar s_{i\cdot T}$, the mean of $k$ specific deviations, stays in the
ranking: its expectation over random tester sets is zero but it is not zero in any
one set. That remainder is what $\rho_k$ of @eq-het-rho-k measures in
@sec-heterosis-step6, so "averaging over testers removes $s_{ij}$" is exact
only for the complete tester set and in expectation otherwise.

Two further limits. First, cross performance is a genotypic value, not a
mid-parent difference, so a testcross mean also carries the candidate's own
additive contribution -- the part that cancelled out of $H$ in the mid-parent
derivation (@eq-het-value) and is not in this decomposition at all. The
row effect of a testcross mean is therefore the sum of that additive part and the
GCA for heterosis, and that sum is the GCA of @eq-hp-gca-sca; what the algebra
here delimits is its dominance part, the GCA for heterosis against the tester pool. Second, $g^A_i$ is defined against the
frequencies $p_B$ of the tester pool. In a recurrent scheme the tester pool is itself
changed by selection from one cycle to the next, so the $g^A_i$ of a candidate in
one cycle is not the quantity it has in the next, and the derivation above is
per cycle.

### SCA is minus twice a weighted parental inner product

The bilinear term is $s_{ij} = -2\sum_k d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\,\delta v_{jk}$: minus
twice the $d$-weighted inner product of the two parents' *centred* genotypes, a
covariance up to the factor $1/m$. For $d_k > 0$, two parents that deviate from
their pools in the same direction have a positive inner product and therefore a
**negative** SCA.

Read in words: two parents that resemble each other -- after removing what is
typical of each pool -- cross badly, and the resemblance that counts is weighted
by $d$, not by marker count. Similarity enters negatively throughout this chapter
-- $1 - \theta_{AB}$, $d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij})$ -- but everywhere else it is
similarity measured against a fixed base. Here it is measured against each pool's
own mean, which is what makes the term specific to a *pair* rather than a
property either parent carries into all its crosses.

It is also @sec-heterosis-distance again. Since $\mu$, $g^A$ and $g^B$ are the
grand, row and column means of the $H_{ij}$ table, $s_{ij}$ is the double-centred
$H$ matrix. Under flat $d$, $H_{ij} = d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij})$, and double-centring
annihilates the constant and flips the sign of what remains (@eq-het-sca-dc, checked in @tbl-het-sca-dc):

$$s_{ij} \;=\; -\,d\,m \cdot \mathrm{DC}\big(f^L\big)_{ij},$$ {#eq-het-sca-dc}

with $\mathrm{DC}(f^L)_{ij} = f^L_{ij} - \bar f^L_{i\cdot} - \bar f^L_{\cdot j} + \bar
f^L_{\cdot\cdot}$ over the $A \times B$ block (row, column and grand means).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-sca-dc
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute difference between the SCA matrix under flat dominance and $-m\\,\\mathrm{DC}(f^L)$ over the $A \\times B$ block (@eq-het-sca-dc), in units of $d$."

s_flat <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, rep(1, ctx$m))$sca
fAB    <- fL[seq_len(nA), nA + seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_B)]
DC_fAB <- fAB - outer(rowMeans(fAB), colMeans(fAB), "+") + mean(fAB)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(s_flat, -ctx$m * DC_fAB, check.attributes = FALSE)))
kv(c(max_residual = max(abs(s_flat + ctx$m * DC_fAB))), sig = TRUE)
```
 The factor $-dm$ is not cosmetic:
$s_{ij}$ is on the trait scale and $f^L$ is a probability, and the minus is the
same minus as in $-2\sum_k d_k \delta u\, \delta v$ -- more coancestry than the
two margins predict means *less* SCA. So the coancestry kernel determines SCA
under exactly the condition it determines heterosis, up to that constant, and
stops doing so under exactly the same condition: a $d$ that varies across loci.

### The variance components

Because the three components are orthogonal, the variance of heterosis over the
factorial splits with them. Under the sampling model of the simulation -- each
line's genotype an independent Bernoulli($p_{Ak}$) draw at every locus, so
unrelated lines and linkage equilibrium within each pool -- each piece has a
closed form in the pool frequencies, compared with the observed variances in
@tbl-het-var-components:

$$\sigma^2_{GCA_A} = \sum_k d_k^2\,(1 - 2p_{Bk})^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{SCA} = 4 \sum_k d_k^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak}\,p_{Bk}q_{Bk}$$ {#eq-het-var-components}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-var-components
#| tbl-cap: "Variance over the full factorial of each combining-ability component of heterosis (@eq-het-gca-sca), observed (divisor $n$) against the closed forms of @eq-het-var-components evaluated at the sample pool frequencies, in squared units of $d$. GCA rows: over the 25 lines of a pool; SCA row: over the 625 crosses. One realisation of the pools (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers) and of $d$ (seed 4)."
qa <- pA * (1 - pA)
qb <- pB * (1 - pB)
pvar <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^2)   # divisor n, as in the closed forms
fmt(data.frame(
  component = c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA"),
  observed  = c(pvar(cs$gca_A), pvar(cs$gca_B), pvar(as.vector(cs$sca))),
  closed_form = c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pB)^2 * qa),
                  sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pA)^2 * qb),
                  4 * sum(d^2 * qa * qb))), 2)
```

The closed forms of @eq-het-var-components take the sample frequencies as the pool frequencies; the observed
column is one realisation of them, computed with divisor $n$ (a population
variance over the lines), which is the divisor the closed forms carry. The GCA rows are variances over
`r book_cfg$n_pool_A` lines, whose relative standard deviation is about
$\sqrt{2/n} \approx$ `r round(100 * sqrt(2 / book_cfg$n_pool_A))` %: one standard
deviation of the statistic, not a tolerance, and the deviations of the observed
variances from the closed forms for these lines are in the last row of
@tbl-het-step7-recycled. That figure belongs to the independent-Bernoulli
sampling model declared immediately above, not to the statistic: it is the
sampling error of a variance over $n$ *independent* observations, and a recycled
pool has no such $n$. @sec-heterosis-step7 measures how the dispersion of that
deviation changes once the lines are related.

Note what each one requires. $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ carries $p_Aq_A\,p_Bq_B$: it needs
**both** pools to be polymorphic. Fix either pool at a locus and that locus
contributes no specific combining ability at all, whatever its $d_k$. Within-pool
diversity is not merely something the diversity constraint defends; it is the
raw material of SCA.

## Divergence destroys SCA faster than it builds GCA {#sec-heterosis-relocation}

Put the two closed forms of @eq-het-var-components next to the drift argument of @sec-heterosis-flat and
the variance tells a different story from the mean. The mean was flat; the
variance is not, and it does not merely change shape.

Under Balding-Nichols, $\mathbb{E}[p_Aq_A] = p^{*}(1-p^{*})(1 - F_{BN})$ and
$\mathbb{E}[(1 - 2p_B)^2] = (1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$, and $p_A$ and $p_B$ are
independent given the ancestral $p^{*}$ (@eq-balding-nichols, stated later, in @sec-simulating-crosses). Per locus, in expectation over the draw,

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}\big] = 4d_k^2\,p^{*2}(1-p^{*})^2\,(1 - F_{BN})^2,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}\big] = d_k^2\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\,(1 - F_{BN})
  \left[(1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\right]$$ {#eq-het-var-bn}

Read the two expressions before reading the sweep, because they already say what
it will show.

Both carry the erosion factor $(1 - F_{BN})$, and both are **zero at
$F_{BN} = 1$**: a pool fixed at every locus has no two lines that differ, so it
has no combining-ability variance of either kind. Divergence therefore cannot
transfer variance from one component to the other indefinitely; it destroys both
in the limit. SCA carries the factor twice, because it needs both pools
polymorphic at the same locus. GCA carries it once, multiplied by the tester
factor $(1 - 2p_B)^2$, whose expectation *grows* with $F_{BN}$.

The two expressions therefore behave differently in $F_{BN}$. The SCA expression
is convex and decreasing on $[0, 1]$: it is a positive constant times
$(1 - F_{BN})^2$, so it only ever falls. The GCA expression is a *concave*
parabola, its $F_{BN}^2$ coefficient being $-4d_k^2p^{*2}_k(1-p^{*}_k)^2$, and
differentiating it gives the only turnover in this section. GCA variance rises
from $F_{BN} = 0$ at a locus if and only if $8p^{*}(1-p^{*}) > 1$, that is
$\tfrac12(1 - 1/\sqrt2) < p^{*} < \tfrac12(1 + 1/\sqrt2)$, and turns over at

$$F^\star_k = \frac{8p^{*}_k(1-p^{*}_k) - 1}{8p^{*}_k(1-p^{*}_k)},$$ {#eq-het-gca-peak}

which is negative outside that interval -- at such loci GCA variance falls from
the start. A sum of concave parabolas is a concave parabola, and its maximum
works out to the $d_k^2\,(p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2$-weighted mean of the $F^\star_k$. Whether
that mean lands inside $[0, 1]$ is a property of the ancestral frequency
distribution, not a theorem: pools founded mostly at extreme frequencies would
put it below zero and GCA variance would decline monotonically. Under the
$U(0.05, 0.95)$ ancestral draw used here enough loci sit in the interval to place
it inside the range, which is why the expected GCA curve of the sweep of
@tbl-het-relocation has an interior peak. The weighted mean locates the peak; a
grid of single draws can bracket it only roughly, because the curve is flat near
the top (see below). With $d$
drawn independently of $p^{*}$ the weight reduces to $(p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2$ in expectation, and
$(p^{*}q^{*})^2 F^\star = p^{*}q^{*}(8p^{*}q^{*} - 1)/8$ (@tbl-het-gca-peak):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-gca-peak
#| tbl-cap: "Expected position of the peak of the GCA variance in divergence: $\\bar F^\\star$ (`expected_GCA_peak_fst`; @eq-het-gca-peak weighted by $(p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2$, ancestral $p^{*}$ uniform on [0.05, 0.95]) and its position on the target-$F_{BN}$ axis of the sweep after the sample-frequency offset (`on_target_axis`; 25 lines per pool). Dimensionless."

pq <- function(p) p * (1 - p)
F_peak <- integrate(function(p) pq(p) * (8 * pq(p) - 1) / 8, 0.05, 0.95)$value /
          integrate(function(p) pq(p)^2, 0.05, 0.95)$value
# the sweep evaluates the closed form at sample frequencies of n inbred lines,
# whose divergence from the ancestral p is F_eff = F + (1 - F)/n; on the
# target-F_BN axis the peak therefore sits at (F_peak - 1/n)/(1 - 1/n)
stopifnot(book_cfg$n_pool_A == book_cfg$n_pool_B)
n_ln <- book_cfg$n_pool_A
F_peak_axis <- (F_peak - 1 / n_ln) / (1 - 1 / n_ln)
kv(c(expected_GCA_peak_fst = F_peak, on_target_axis = F_peak_axis), 3)
```

Call this weighted mean $\bar F^\star$; here $\bar F^\star =$
`r round(F_peak, 3)`. It is the turnover in the divergence, from the ancestral
frequencies, of whatever frequencies the closed form is evaluated at. The sweep of
@tbl-het-relocation evaluates it at frequencies estimated from $n =$ `r book_cfg$n_pool_A`
inbred lines per pool. Given the ancestral $p^{*}$, such an estimate has variance
$p^{*}q^{*}F_{BN} + \mathbb{E}[p_{\mathrm{pool}}q_{\mathrm{pool}}]/n = p^{*}q^{*}\,[F_{BN} + (1 - F_{BN})/n]$,
so its divergence is $F_{\mathrm{eff}} = F_{BN} + (1 - F_{BN})/n$, not the target
$F_{BN}$ -- the same sampling term sized for the mean in @sec-heterosis-flat. On
the target-$F_{BN}$ axis of the sweep the expected peak is therefore
$(\bar F^\star - 1/n)/(1 - 1/n) =$ `r round(F_peak_axis, 3)`.


What is monotone is the ratio (@eq-het-sca-gca-ratio),


$$\frac{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}]}{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}]}
  = \frac{4p^{*}(1-p^{*})\,(1 - F_{BN})}{(1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})},$$ {#eq-het-sca-gca-ratio}

which falls in $F_{BN}$ at every locus. So the defensible statement is about the
*share*, not about a transfer. Expected heterosis, we already know, is flat in
$F_{BN}$. Sweeping the pools apart -- same ancestral frequencies, fresh
Balding-Nichols draws at each `fst`, as in @sec-heterosis-flat -- and evaluating
the closed forms on the realised frequencies (@tbl-het-relocation,
@fig-heterosis-relocation):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-relocation
#| tbl-cap: "Closed-form variances of heterosis over the factorial (@eq-het-var-components) along the neutral sweep of @tbl-het-sweep, evaluated at the realised pool frequencies of each draw, in squared units of $d$. `var_GCA`: sum of both pools' GCA variances; `var_SCA`: SCA variance; `frac_SCA`: SCA share of their sum. One draw per row (seed 5 for the pools, seed 4 for $d$), no replication; the grid maximum over pool seeds 1 to 20 is given in the text."
grid_fst <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45)
reloc <- function(fst, seed = 5) {              # pool seed 5 is the chapter's draw
  cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = seed))
  Pf <- pool_freqs(simulate_lines(cf) / 2,
                   rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B)))
  a <- Pf["A", ]; b <- Pf["B", ]
  va <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * b)^2 * a * (1 - a))
  vb <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * a)^2 * b * (1 - b))
  vs <- 4 * sum(d^2 * a * (1 - a) * b * (1 - b))
  data.frame(fst = fst, var_GCA = va + vb, var_SCA = vs,
             frac_SCA = vs / (va + vb + vs))
}
rl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc))
# Grid maximum of the GCA curve for pool seeds 1 to 20 (the position of the
# maximum is a property of the draw; the expected peak is not).
peak_by_seed <- vapply(1:20, function(sd_) {
  r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc, seed = sd_))
  r$fst[which.max(r$var_GCA)]
}, numeric(1))
pk_tab   <- table(peak_by_seed)
peak_txt <- paste0(sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(names(pk_tab))), " in ", pk_tab,
                   collapse = ", ")
stopifnot(F_peak_axis > min(grid_fst), F_peak_axis < max(grid_fst),
          F_peak_axis > min(peak_by_seed), F_peak_axis < max(peak_by_seed),
          identical(rl, do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc, seed = 5))))
fmt(rl, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heterosis-relocation
#| fig-cap: "The same neutral divergence sweep, read through the combining-ability decomposition rather than through the mean: closed-form variances of heterosis over the factorial (@eq-het-var-components), evaluated at the realised pool frequencies of each draw, in squared units of $d$, against the target Balding-Nichols `fst` ($F_{BN}$). GCA is the sum of both pools' GCA variances. One draw per point (seed 5 for the pools, seed 4 for $d$; 25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), no replication; values in @tbl-het-relocation."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the variance of heterosis over the factorial against target fst from 0.02 to 0.45. The SCA variance falls steeply across the whole range; the GCA variance of both pools rises much less, peaks inside the range and turns down."
plot(rl$fst, rl$var_GCA, type = "b", pch = 19, col = book_pal[["ink"]],
     ylim = range(0, rl$var_GCA, rl$var_SCA),
     xlab = expression("target " * F[BN] * " between pools"),
     ylab = expression("variance of heterosis over the factorial (units of " * d^2 * ")"))
lines(rl$fst, rl$var_SCA, type = "b", pch = 15, col = book_pal[["mid"]])
legend("right", c("GCA (both pools)", "SCA"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       pch = c(19, 15), col = book_pal[c("ink", "mid")])
grid()
```

Take the three columns in order, because the headline is in the arithmetic
between them.

SCA variance falls by
