`r round(100 * (1 - rl$var_SCA[nrow(rl)] / rl$var_SCA[1]))` % across the sweep, a
drop of `r round(rl$var_SCA[1] - rl$var_SCA[nrow(rl)], 1)` units. GCA variance
ends `r round(100 * (rl$var_GCA[nrow(rl)] / rl$var_GCA[1] - 1))` % above where it
started, a gain of `r round(rl$var_GCA[nrow(rl)] - rl$var_GCA[1], 1)` units, and
has its largest value on this grid at an `fst` of
`r rl$fst[which.max(rl$var_GCA)]`. The position of the grid maximum is a property of
this draw, not of the model: repeating the sweep for pool seeds 1 to
`r length(peak_by_seed)` on the same grid and the same $d$, the grid maximum fell at
`r peak_txt`. The curve is flat near its top, so a grid of single draws locates the
peak only to the range of those values. What the model gives is the expected peak on
this axis, computed from @eq-het-gca-peak with the sample-frequency offset above,
`r round(F_peak_axis, 2)`, which lies inside that range. So the GCA gain recovers about
`r round(100 * (rl$var_GCA[nrow(rl)] - rl$var_GCA[1]) / (rl$var_SCA[1] - rl$var_SCA[nrow(rl)]))` %
of what SCA lost. The rest is gone: total variance in heterosis over the
factorial falls from `r round(rl$var_GCA[1] + rl$var_SCA[1], 1)` to
`r round(rl$var_GCA[nrow(rl)] + rl$var_SCA[nrow(rl)], 1)`, a
`r round(100 * (1 - (rl$var_GCA[nrow(rl)] + rl$var_SCA[nrow(rl)]) / (rl$var_GCA[1] + rl$var_SCA[1])))` %
decline, while the mean stays fixed throughout.

Read those four percentages as one realisation, not as constants. They come from
a single pair of seeds -- `seed = 5` for the pool frequencies, `set.seed(4)` for
$d$ -- with no replication and no dispersion reported, and they will move if
either changes. What does not depend on the seed is the direction, which is
already in @eq-het-var-bn: $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ is a positive multiple of
$(1 - F_{BN})^2$ and can only fall, and both components vanish at $F_{BN} = 1$,
so no amount of neutral divergence can hold the total up. The ordering of the
columns is algebra; their magnitudes are this draw.

The share of that variance which is specific falls from
`r round(rl$frac_SCA[1], 3)` to `r round(rl$frac_SCA[nrow(rl)], 3)`. That
statement -- about the share -- is the one the sweep supports; "the dominance
expressed as SCA reappears as GCA" is not, and the two variance columns of
@tbl-het-relocation are why.

The share result itself is not new in direction. @reif2007 prove that the ratio
of dominance to additive variance in a hybrid population falls as its two parent
populations diverge, and conclude that superior hybrids then become predictable
from general combining ability effects. The direction of this section's share
result is theirs; the quantity is not the same one. Their ratio is
$\sigma^2_D / \sigma^2_A$ over the hybrid population, whose denominator contains
the additive variance contributed by the parents -- the part that cancelled out
of $H$ in the mid-parent derivation (@eq-het-value) and is absent from everything computed here.
The ratio in @tbl-het-relocation (`frac_SCA`) is $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ over
$\sigma^2_{GCA_A} + \sigma^2_{GCA_B} + \sigma^2_{SCA}$ *within heterosis only*. The two move the same
way and are not interchangeable. What the sweep adds is the denominator, which a
ratio hides: a ratio can fall because its
numerator falls, because its denominator rises, or both, and the columns of
@tbl-het-relocation say which. Here the numerator collapses and the denominator recovers only part of
it, so the share falls and the total falls with it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Neutral divergence shrinks the part of hybrid variation that only a cross can reveal

*Neutral* divergence -- drift, the only kind on this sweep -- does not buy
expected heterosis, and it does not move heterosis from one combining-ability
component into the other. It **shrinks the part of hybrid variation that only a
cross can reveal**, destroying SCA variance faster than it builds GCA variance.
An additive model looks better against diverged pools mainly because there is
less left for it to miss. Divergence that is *aligned* with dominance is a
different matter and @sec-heterosis-alignment is where it is measured; the
sweep here holds alignment at zero by construction.
:::

This sharpens a question @sec-genomic-prediction will have to leave open. That
chapter fits one additive effect per marker and notes that such a model cannot represent
SCA at all. The sweep says how large the unrepresentable share is, and how it
moves: against poorly separated pools most of the variance in heterosis is
specific; against well separated ones a minority is. These are shares of the
variance in *heterosis*, not of total hybrid value, whose parental-mean part is
additive at every $F_{BN}$. The nearest empirical statement this chapter can cite is
that of @technow2014, for Dent and Flint heterotic groups: they report that the
contribution of SCA variance to total genetic variance was comparatively small in
their data, and high prediction accuracy from models that include GCA effects (their
genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) model fitted GCA and SCA terms and their BayesB model additive and dominance
effects, so that accuracy is not that of an additive model). The sentence that
follows from this chapter is that a small SCA share in well-separated groups is
consistent with the mechanism of this section. The quantities differ -- their share
is of total genetic variance, this chapter's is of the variance in heterosis -- and
a single observational study in one crop cannot test the mechanism.

:::: {.callout-warning}
## A smaller SCA share is not a better programme, and this is not a licence to maximise $F_{ST}$

Three things stay true at every point on that sweep, all of them in expectation over
the draw of the pools (the sweep itself is one draw per point). Expected heterosis does not
change. The gene diversity spent to buy
the divergence is spent for good: $GD_T$ falls by what $GD_{BS}$ gains, and
$GD_{WS}$ by twice that (@sec-heterosis-flat). And $\sigma^2_{SCA} \to 0$ is the limit in which no cross is better than its
parents predict -- there is nothing left to *find* by testing combinations, which
is the activity the whole factorial exists to support. Past the peak of the GCA
curve in @fig-heterosis-relocation even the predictable part, the GCA variance,
shrinks: at
$F_{BN} = 1$ there is no
combining-ability variance of either kind, because no two lines in a pool differ.

The falling SCA share is therefore a fact about what a predictor can express, not
a gain. A programme reading it as one would be congratulating itself on having
less to predict.

So this is a second reason, independent of the diversity-side one, for the prescription
@sec-stages Trap 3 will make, to hold the statistic $F_{ST}$ in a band rather than at a maximum. @sec-heterosis-flat gave the
diversity-side reason. This is the prediction-side one, and it points the same
way.
::::

### What this says about ranking crosses

The F1 of two fixed lines is genetically uniform, so the progeny-variance term
that drives the usefulness criterion of stage S2 (@tbl-hp-stages; the criterion is
set out in @sec-stages) is zero for the hybrid itself, and cross ranking reduces to ranking means. That is true, and it is why
this book ranks hybrids on an index rather than on $\mu + i h \sigma$.

It does not follow that the ranking is easy. The *mean* of an F1 contains an SCA
term that an additive $\mathbf{G}$ omits entirely, and @sec-heterosis-relocation
sized its share of the variance in heterosis: a majority of it against weakly
separated pools, a minority against well separated ones, and zero only where, at
every locus, at least one of the two pools is fixed -- one pool fixed everywhere
is a special case of that, not the condition. The
progeny variance collapses; the specific combining ability in the mean does not.

## Running this on a real programme {#sec-heterosis-protocol}

Eight steps, in the order they have to be executed on a maize-type programme's
own data. Each one names the function to call, the quantity to check and what
failure looks like. Steps 1-5 need only genotypes and pool labels. In every
**Call** line `GL` is the line genotype matrix coded 0/1, the package convention
for line-level functions; this chapter's `simulate_lines()` returns 0/2, which is
why its code passes `L / 2`. Data coded 0/1/2 must be halved once, before step 1,
and never again.

Steps 6-8 need more, and the requirement is worth naming because it is the
reason these steps are rarely run. $H_{ij}$ is a **mid-parent difference**, so
fitting the decomposition on real data needs the hybrid trial *and* per-se
phenotypes of the parent lines, measured on the same scale as the hybrid trial:
a separate inbred-level trial, in the same environments, with a common check set
or an overlapping design to put the two on one scale. Very few programmes run
one, because inbred per-se performance has no commercial value. Without it what
the two-way layout of step 6 fits is hybrid *performance*, not heterosis, and
its row effects are the GCA of @eq-hp-gca-sca: the GCA for heterosis of
@sec-heterosis-gca-sca **plus** the parent's own additive contribution
$\sum_k a_k\,\delta u_{ik}$, the term that is not in $H$ at all. Both
decompositions are legitimate; they are not the same decomposition, and the
difference is exactly the parental additive part.

### Step 1 -- Verify the parents are inbred, and price it if they are not {#sec-heterosis-step1}

Every formula in this chapter rests on the premise that the parents are fully inbred (@sec-heterosis-premises). It is checkable in one
line: an inbred line's self-coancestry is exactly 1, and its heterozygous
fraction exactly 0 (@tbl-het-step1-check).


```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step1-check
#| tbl-cap: "Check of the inbred premise on the simulated lines (25 + 25, coded 0/1): smallest self-coancestry, largest fraction of heterozygous loci in any line, and largest absolute dominance value, `heterosis_value()`, of any line (units of $d$)."

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2)), rep(1, nrow(L)),
                           check.attributes = FALSE)),
          max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d))) == 0)
kv(c(min_self_coancestry = min(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2))),
     max_het_fraction    = max(rowMeans(L / 2 == 0.5)),
     dominance_value_of_the_most_heterozygous_line =
       max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d)))))
```

If those numbers are not 1, 0 and 0, the parents are not fixed and the mid-parent
already carries dominance of its own. On the simulated lines they are 1, 0 and 0 by
construction, since the matrix is coded 0/1; the check is meaningful on real data. The size of the resulting error is not
small. Build parents that are *intra-pool* F1s instead of inbred lines -- one
random cross within each pool, so each parent sits at its pool's random-mating
heterozygosity -- then cross them across pools by drawing one gamete per parent
per locus (@tbl-het-step1-noninbred):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step1-noninbred
#| tbl-cap: "Intra-pool F1 parents (one random cross within each pool per parent, 25 + 25 parents, seeds 101 and 102) crossed over the full A x B factorial with one gamete per parent per locus, five independent gamete draws (seeds 201 to 205), $d_k$ as drawn for the chapter (seed 4). `parent_het_fraction`: fraction of parental loci heterozygous; `closed_form`: `heterosis_expected()` at the parents' pool frequencies (@eq-het-expected); `simulated_hybrid`, `simulated_gain`: mean dominance value of the hybrids, and mean hybrid minus mid-parent, averaged over the five draws; `sd_across_draws`: s.d. over draws of the mean hybrid value, equal for the gain because the parental term is fixed; `exact_sum_d_y2`: $\\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ at the inbred lines' pool frequencies; `overstatement`: `closed_form` over `simulated_gain`. `unit` gives the unit of each row; `d` is the dominance-effect scale of the chapter."
intra_pool_f1 <- function(W, n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  (W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ] + W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ]) / 2
}
ZA  <- intra_pool_f1(U, nrow(U), 101)
ZB  <- intra_pool_f1(V, nrow(V), 102)
pd2 <- expand.grid(a = seq_len(nrow(ZA)), b = seq_len(nrow(ZB)))

# One gamete per parent per locus, five independent draws of the whole factorial.
draw <- t(vapply(seq_len(5), function(r) {
  set.seed(200 + r)
  gA <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZA), 1, ZA), nrow(ZA))[pd2$a, ]
  gB <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZB), 1, ZB), nrow(ZB))[pd2$b, ]
  H  <- heterosis_value((gA + gB) / 2, d)
  mp <- (heterosis_value(ZA, d)[pd2$a] + heterosis_value(ZB, d)[pd2$b]) / 2
  c(hybrid_value = mean(H), mid_parent_gain = mean(H - mp))
}, numeric(2)))

closed_form <- heterosis_expected(colMeans(ZA), colMeans(ZB), d)
fmt(data.frame(quantity = c("parent_het_fraction", "closed_form", "simulated_hybrid",
                            "simulated_gain", "sd_across_draws", "exact_sum_d_y2",
                            "overstatement"),
               value = c(mean(c(ZA, ZB) == 0.5), closed_form,
                         mean(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]),
                         # parental term fixed across draws: same s.d. for the gain
                         sd(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), sum(d * (pA - pB)^2),
                         closed_form / mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"])),
               unit = c("fraction", rep("sum over loci, in d", 5), "ratio")), 3)
```

Result. The parents carry
`r fmt(mean(c(ZA, ZB) == 0.5), 3)` of their loci heterozygous.
`heterosis_expected()` is still correct about the *hybrid*: it predicts
`r fmt(closed_form, 1)` against a simulated
`r fmt(mean(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), 1)` (s.d. `r fmt(sd(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), 2)`
over five gamete draws), because that formula uses gamete frequencies only and
does not care what the parents' own genotypes are. What it is not correct about
is the *gain*: the mid-parent difference is
`r fmt(mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]), 1)`, the same
`r fmt(sd(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), 2)` standard deviation shifted down by the
parents' own dominance value, so reading the closed form as heterosis overstates
the gain by a factor of
`r fmt(closed_form / mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]), 2)`. The simulated gain
agrees with the exact $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ of
@sec-heterosis-identity, `r fmt(sum(d * (pA - pB)^2), 1)`, to within one
standard deviation of the gamete draw.

Interpretation, with its limit. The correction is not a fudge factor: it is the
parents' own dominance contribution,
`r fmt(mean(draw[, "hybrid_value"]) - mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]), 1)` here,
which `heterosis_value()` computes on the parent matrix directly and which is
exactly zero under the inbred premise. Subtracting it recovers the mid-parent
gain, and that gain matches the $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ of @sec-heterosis-identity
**in expectation only**: the realised intra-pool F1 parents are one draw, not
their own expectation, so each replicate's mid-parent carries a sampling
deviation of its own -- which is why the agreement reported above is to within
one standard deviation of the gamete draw and not exact. The factor of
`r fmt(closed_form / mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]), 2)` itself is specific to
this configuration -- `fst` = `r book_cfg$fst`, gamma-distributed $d$, parents at
full random-mating heterozygosity -- and it shrinks toward 1 as the parents
approach fixation. Five gamete draws at one seed family give the dispersion
reported and no more.

**Call.** `diag(molecular_coancestry(GL))`; `heterosis_value()` on the parent
matrix, not only on the hybrids.
**Check.** Self-coancestry 1 and heterozygous fraction 0 for every parent.
**Warning sign.** Any parent with a heterozygous fraction above the marker error
rate. Partially inbred parents (one or two generations of selfing, clonal maintenance of a heterozygous
plant) invalidate the mid-parent cancellation, not the hybrid prediction.
**Threshold.** `heterosis_value()` on the parent set must return zero to machine
precision. If it does not, subtract it: the mid-parent gain is the hybrid value
minus the parents' mean, always.

### Step 2 -- Compute pool frequencies, and keep them distinct from $p_0$ {#sec-heterosis-step2}

`pool_freqs(GL, pool)` returns one row per pool. These are the *current* cycle's
frequencies and they are supposed to move; they are not the frozen base $p_0$
against which the two inbreeding lenses (defined in @sec-hp-inbreeding, measured in
@sec-genomic-era) are measured; $p_0$ is defined in @sec-hp-popgen. Both objects
are frequency vectors over the same markers and confusing them produces a
heterosis prediction anchored to a population that no longer exists.

**Call.** `pool_freqs(GL, pool)` on the current cycle's line matrix.
**Check.** `nrow() == 2` and the pool labels are the heterotic groups, not
families or locations.
**Warning sign.** A pool frequency vector computed over *hybrids* rather than
lines. On the full factorial that gives $(p_A + p_B)/2$ for both pools --
@sec-era-step1 checks the identity on selected sets -- which sets $y \equiv 0$ and reports the
divergence term as zero.
**Threshold.** None; this is a bookkeeping step, and the only failure is silent.

### Step 3 -- Decide what stands in for $d_k$, and say so {#sec-heterosis-step3}

Nothing below step 4 can be computed without a weight per locus. Three defensible
choices, in decreasing order of what they require:

1. **Estimated $d_k$** from a dominance model fitted on hybrid data. This is what
   the premise that the marker panel is the set of dominance loci (@sec-heterosis-premises) assumes exists, and it is the only option that lets
   $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ be computed.
2. **Flat $d_k \equiv 1$**, which makes $H$ proportional to marker distance and
   the whole calculation a function of the coancestry kernel
   (@sec-heterosis-distance). Everything in this chapter's frequency algebra
   still holds; what is lost is alignment, which is exactly the term flat $d$
   sets to zero.
3. **No $d$ at all**, reporting only $GD_{BS}$ and `mean_sq_delta_p`, which is
   the frequency half of the divergence term and is exact
   (@sec-heterosis-alignment says what is missing).

The cost of choice 2 is measurable, and it is the correlation already computed
in @sec-heterosis-distance: under flat $d$ heterosis and marker distance are the
same statistic, and under the gamma-distributed $d$ used here the correlation
between them is `r round(cor(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d), 1 - fL[ab]), 2)`.

**Call.** `heterosis_value(X, d)` with whichever vector you have chosen, and
record the choice next to the number.
**Check.** `length(d) == ncol(X)` and $d$ indexed in the same marker order.
**Warning sign.** A report that gives expected heterosis without saying which of
the three choices produced it. At the correlation just quoted the choices are not
interchangeable for ranking crosses, and their absolute values are on different
scales altogether.
**Threshold.** If choice 2 is used, state that alignment is assumed zero, because
that is what flat $d$ asserts.

### Step 4 -- Partition, and cross-check against the diversity partition {#sec-heterosis-step4}

`heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d)` returns `shared`, `divergence` and `total`.
With $d \equiv 1$ and divided by $m$ the first two are the $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$
of `gd_partition()`, and the chunk in @sec-heterosis-identity asserts that to a relative
tolerance of `1e-12`. Running both is a consistency test worth the two lines it costs --
but only if the two calls are given the **same line weights**, and by default
they are not.

The algebra says why. For any weights $\mathbf{w}_A$ over the lines of pool A
summing to 1 within the pool (`line_weights()` rescales usage this way), with
inbred lines, $\theta_A = \overline{p_{A,w}^2 + q_{A,w}^2}$ where
$p_{A,w} = \sum_i w_{A,i} u_{ik}$ is the *weighted* pool frequency, and the same
for $B$ and for $\theta_{AB}$. Substituting into `gd_partition()`'s definitions,
$GD_T = 1 - \bar f = \overline{2\bar p(1 - \bar p)}$ and
$GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f = \overline{(p_{A,w} - p_{B,w})^2}/2$, which are
exactly `heterosis_partition()`'s two terms evaluated at $p_{A,w}$ and
$p_{B,w}$. So the identity holds for *any* weighting -- as long as both sides use
the same one. `gd_partition(idx, ctx)` weights each line by how often the
selection uses it (`line_weights()`), while `pool_freqs()` is unweighted. On the
full factorial usage is uniform and the two coincide; on a selected subset they
do not, and the discrepancy is not small (@tbl-het-step4-usage; the usage of the selection is in @tbl-het-step4-balance):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step4-usage
#| tbl-cap: "Shared and divergence terms per locus ($d_k \\equiv 1$) for one 60-hybrid index-truncation selection, from four sets of pool frequencies: all lines unweighted, the lines used unweighted, usage-weighted (`line_weights()`), and $GD_T$, $GD_{BS}$ of `gd_partition()` on the same selection. Error columns: per cent deviation from `gd_partition()`."
i_trunc <- sel_truncation(ctx, 60)     # index truncation: deliberately unbalanced
gp_sel  <- gd_partition(i_trunc, ctx)
GLh <- L / 2
wt  <- line_weights(i_trunc, ctx)
hp2 <- function(a, b) {
  heterosis_partition(a, b, rep(1, ctx$m))[c("shared", "divergence")] / ctx$m
}
cmp <- rbind(
  `all lines, unweighted`  = hp2(pA, pB),
  `lines used, unweighted` = hp2(colMeans(GLh[unique(ctx$ped$a[i_trunc]), ]),
                                 colMeans(GLh[unique(ctx$ped$b[i_trunc]), ])),
  `usage-weighted`         = hp2(as.vector(wt[["A"]] %*% GLh),
                                 as.vector(wt[["B"]] %*% GLh)),
  `gd_partition(idx, ctx)` = c(gp_sel[["GD_T"]], gp_sel[["GD_BS"]]))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(cmp["usage-weighted", ]),
                           c(gp_sel[["GD_T"]], gp_sel[["GD_BS"]]))))
# theta_AB uses weights rescaled to 1 within each pool, not the global block
pAw <- as.vector(wt[["A"]] %*% GLh); pBw <- as.vector(wt[["B"]] %*% GLh)
th_AB <- theta_pools(i_trunc, ctx)[["theta_AB"]]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(th_AB, mean(pAw * pBw + (1 - pAw) * (1 - pBw)))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(th_AB / 4, drop((wt[["A"]] / 2) %*% ctx[["fL"]] %*% (wt[["B"]] / 2)))))
fmt(data.frame(cmp,
               shared_err_pct     = 100 * (cmp[, "shared"] / gp_sel[["GD_T"]] - 1),
               divergence_err_pct = 100 * (cmp[, "divergence"] / gp_sel[["GD_BS"]] - 1)), 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step4-balance
#| tbl-cap: "Line usage of the 60-hybrid index-truncation selection of @tbl-het-step4-usage: distinct pool-A and pool-B lines among its parents, the largest number of the selected crosses any one line enters, and the number of hybrids selected (counts)."

kv(c(lines_used_A = length(unique(ctx$ped$a[i_trunc])),
     lines_used_B = length(unique(ctx$ped$b[i_trunc])),
     max_line_use = max_line_use(i_trunc, ctx), n_sel = length(i_trunc)), 0)
```

Result. With usage weights on both sides the identity is exact to machine
precision -- the `stopifnot()` enforces it -- while the unweighted pool
frequencies of `pool_freqs()` overstate `shared` by
`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (cmp["all lines, unweighted", "shared"] / gp_sel[["GD_T"]] - 1))` %
and understate `divergence` by
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(100 * (cmp["all lines, unweighted", "divergence"] / gp_sel[["GD_BS"]] - 1)))` %
on this 60-hybrid truncation set, which uses only
`r length(unique(ctx$ped$a[i_trunc]))` pool-A lines with one of them in
`r max_line_use(i_trunc, ctx)` of the 60 crosses. Restricting the unweighted mean to
the lines actually used recovers part of the gap and not the rest, because the
usage *within* the used set is itself far from uniform.

Interpretation. The two functions are not inconsistent; they answer the same
question on two different populations -- a notional pool in which every line is
equally represented, and the pool as the selection actually weights it. Which one
a report wants depends on the question, and the only error is comparing one with
the other and calling the difference a bug. The order of magnitude quoted here is
one selection at one scale; a plan with a usage cap (`max_use`) sits between the
two rows.

**Call.** `heterosis_partition()` on the pool frequencies and
`gd_partition(idx, ctx)` on the hybrid set -- with the pool frequencies weighted
by `line_weights(idx, ctx)` if the two are to be compared at all.
**Check.** `shared / m == GD_T` and `divergence / m == GD_BS` under flat $d$,
**both computed from usage-weighted pool frequencies**. On the full factorial,
or under any uniform usage, the unweighted `pool_freqs()` satisfies this too.
**Warning sign.** A disagreement on a selected subset is almost always the
weighting above, not a coding error: check `line_weights()` first, and only then
whether the lines are coded 0/1 or the pool labels differ between the calls.
A $GD_{WI}$ that is not zero is the separate failure -- with inbred parents it
must be, and a non-zero value means the line matrix contains heterozygotes, back
to step 1.
**Threshold.** Machine precision when both sides carry the same weights. With
unweighted pool frequencies against a selected subset, expect tens of per cent on
the divergence term, of the size measured above, and do not treat it as a
tolerance to tighten.

### Step 5 -- Log `mean_sq_delta_p` every cycle {#sec-heterosis-step5}

`s1_monitor(GL, pool, cycle)` is the per-cycle panel. Of its three
complementarity columns only `mean_sq_delta_p` is exact -- it is $\overline{y^2}$, so
half of it is $GD_{BS}$ -- and `frac_opposite_fixed` is zero across most of the
useful range, as the sweep in @sec-heterosis-flat shows.

**Call.** `s1_monitor()` once per cycle, appended to a single data frame.
**Check.** `mean_sq_delta_p / 2` against `gd_partition()`'s `GD_BS`, on the full
factorial, where line usage is uniform. On a selected subset the two agree only
if the pool frequencies are usage-weighted (@sec-heterosis-step4); with the
unweighted frequencies `s1_monitor()` uses, expect a gap of the size measured
there.
**Warning sign.** `frac_opposite_fixed` used as the divergence statistic. In the
sweep of @sec-heterosis-flat it is exactly zero at every `fst` up to 0.10 -- not
one marker in `r book_cfg$m` -- while over the same span the divergence term has
already risen by a factor of
`r fmt(sw$divergence[sw$fst == 0.10] / sw$divergence[sw$fst == 0.02], 2)`
(`r fmt(sw$divergence[sw$fst == 0.02], 4)` to
`r fmt(sw$divergence[sw$fst == 0.10], 4)` per locus at $d = 1$). The first
non-zero grid point is at `fst` =
`r sw$fst[which(sw$frac_opposite_fixed > 0)[1]]`, by which point divergence has
risen `r fmt(sw$divergence[which(sw$frac_opposite_fixed > 0)[1]] / sw$divergence[1], 1)`-fold.
**Threshold.** A *band* on $F_{ST}$, not a maximum. @sec-heterosis-flat gives
the diversity-side reason and @sec-heterosis-relocation the prediction-side one.

### Step 6 -- Check that the crossing layout identifies what you intend to fit {#sec-heterosis-step6}

This is the step most often skipped, and it is arithmetic, not opinion. The
general rule -- a crossing plan as a bipartite graph, the rank of the GCA design
matrix as lines minus connected components, and the accuracy of a testcross mean
against the number of testers with plot error included -- is developed in the
Mating and testing design part, later, at @sec-mating-connectivity and
@sec-mating-tester. This step keeps only what the heterosis decomposition adds:
the layout check on the chapter's own factorial, and the finite-population
correction for drawing testers from a pool of $n_B$. In this step $k$ is the number
of testers, as in @sec-mating-tester; everywhere else in the chapter it indexes
loci. The decomposition
$H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}$ is the two-way layout with identified rows
and columns. Count the degrees of freedom the layout actually provides (@tbl-het-step6-layout):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step6-layout
#| tbl-cap: "Degrees of freedom of the two-way layout when all 25 pool-A lines are crossed to the first 1, 2, 5 or 25 pool-B testers, one observation per cross. `rank_mu_gca`: rank of the design matrix with mean and GCA effects; `rank_with_sca`: rank with the GCA x GCA interaction added; `sca_df`: their difference; `residual_df`: crosses minus the saturated rank."
layout_df <- function(n_testers) {
  k <- which(ib <= n_testers)
  a <- factor(ia[k]); b <- factor(ib[k])
  X_add <- if (n_testers > 1) model.matrix(~ a + b) else model.matrix(~ a)
  X_sat <- if (n_testers > 1) model.matrix(~ a * b) else X_add
  data.frame(testers = n_testers, crosses = length(k),
             rank_mu_gca = qr(X_add)$rank, rank_with_sca = qr(X_sat)$rank,
             sca_df = qr(X_sat)$rank - qr(X_add)$rank,
             residual_df = length(k) - qr(X_sat)$rank)
}
fmt(do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 2, 5, book_cfg$n_pool_B), layout_df)))
```

Result. With a single tester the $\mu + g^A$ model already has rank equal to the
number of crosses, so `sca_df` is 0: specific combining ability is not
estimable, not merely imprecise. From two testers onward `sca_df` is positive.
`residual_df` is 0 in every row, because there is one observation per cross --
SCA becomes *identifiable* from the layout at two testers and *testable* only
when the trial adds replication.

How much a small tester set costs for general combining ability is a separate
question with a closed-form answer. Averaging a pool-A line over $k$ testers
leaves it with $g^A_i$ plus the mean of $k$ specific deviations, so the
correlation between the testcross mean and the true $g^A$ is

$$\rho_k = \left[1 + \frac{\sigma^2_{SCA}}{\sigma^2_{GCA_A}}
        \cdot \frac{n_B - k}{k\,(n_B - 1)}\right]^{-1/2}$$ {#eq-het-rho-k}

where the second factor is the finite-population correction for drawing $k$ of
the $n_B$ available testers without replacement; at $k = n_B$ it vanishes and
$\rho_k = 1$ exactly, because the row mean of the complete factorial *is*
$\mu + g^A_i$. This is the least-squares accuracy $\rho$ of @sec-mating-tester
with $\sigma^2_g = \sigma^2_{GCA_A}$, $\sigma^2_s = \sigma^2_{SCA}$, $c = k$ and
no plot error ($\sigma^2_e = 0$, since $H$ here is known exactly); as
$n_B \to \infty$ the correction tends to $1/k$ and the two expressions coincide.
Many random tester sets per $k$ (@tbl-het-step6-testers):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step6-testers
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation between a pool-A line's mean heterosis over $k$ randomly drawn pool-B testers and its $g^A_i$: mean and s.d. over 4000 tester sets per $k$ (`cor_mean`, `cor_sd`), the closed form $\\rho_k$ of @eq-het-rho-k (`predicted`), and the residual `cor_mean` minus `predicted` in standard errors of the mean, `cor_sd` over the square root of the number of sets (`resid_se`; NA at $k = n_B = 25$, where only one tester set exists). One realisation of the pools and of $d$."
Htab  <- matrix(H, nA, book_cfg$n_pool_B)   # rows = pool A, columns = pool B
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(Htab, cs$mu + outer(cs$gca_A, cs$gca_B, "+") + cs$sca)))
v_gca <- pvar(cs$gca_A)                     # divisor n, as rho_k assumes
v_sca <- pvar(as.vector(cs$sca))
nBt   <- book_cfg$n_pool_B
n_sets <- 4000
tester_scan <- function(k, reps = n_sets) {
  r <- vapply(seq_len(reps), function(i) {
    set.seed(55 + 100000 * k + i)               # 1000 * k would collide across k
    cor(rowMeans(Htab[, sample.int(nBt, k), drop = FALSE]), cs$gca_A)
  }, numeric(1))
  data.frame(testers = k, cor_mean = mean(r), cor_sd = sd(r),
             predicted = 1 / sqrt(1 + (v_sca / v_gca) * (nBt - k) / (k * (nBt - 1))))
}
ts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, nBt), tester_scan))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == nBt], 1)))
# The residual is only interpretable where the tester sets differ at all; at
# k = n_B there is one possible set, so cor_sd is a rounding residue and the
# ratio would be 0/0 dressed up as a number.
ts$resid_se <- ifelse(ts$cor_sd > 1e-12,
                      (ts$cor_mean - ts$predicted) / (ts$cor_sd / sqrt(n_sets)), NA)
fmt(ts, 4)
```

Result. A single tester ranks pool-A lines for general combining ability with a
correlation of `r fmt(ts$cor_mean[1], 2)` (s.d. `r fmt(ts$cor_sd[1], 2)` over
`r n_sets` tester choices); five testers give `r fmt(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == 5], 2)`
and ten give `r fmt(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == 10], 2)`. The mean over tester sets
and the closed form differ by at most
`r fmt(max(abs(ts$cor_mean - ts$predicted)), 3)` at any $k$. At $k = 1$ the
difference is `r fmt(abs(ts$resid_se[ts$testers == 1]), 2)` standard errors of the mean;
at $k = 2, 3, 5, 10$ the mean lies above the closed form by
`r fmt(min((ts$cor_mean - ts$predicted)[ts$testers %in% c(2, 3, 5, 10)]), 3)` to
`r fmt(max((ts$cor_mean - ts$predicted)[ts$testers %in% c(2, 3, 5, 10)]), 3)`, which is
`r fmt(min(ts$resid_se[ts$testers %in% c(2, 3, 5, 10)]), 1)` to
`r fmt(max(ts$resid_se[ts$testers %in% c(2, 3, 5, 10)]), 1)` standard errors. The
closed form is therefore exact at $k = 1$ within the noise of this scan and
understates the mean correlation slightly, by a few thousandths, for $k$ between 2
and 10.

Reading of the residuals, and its limit. The deviations are small against the quantity
being predicted and the closed form is adequate to size a tester set; this section
does not claim it is exact. Two possible reasons for the sign are not tested here:
$\rho_k$ is a function of an *expected* sampling variance, whereas
@tbl-het-step6-testers averages correlations, and $x \mapsto (1 + x)^{-1/2}$ is
convex, which by Jensen's inequality would put the mean of the correlations above
the function of the mean; and $\mathrm{cov}_i(g^A_i, \overline{s}_{i\cdot})$
vanishes only when the mean runs over all $n_B$ testers, not over a subset. The scan
is a measurement on one realisation of the pools and of $d$, with the dispersion
over tester sets reported, not a validation of the formula at other pools.

Interpretation. The whole scan is driven by one ratio,
$\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA_A} =$ `r fmt(v_sca / v_gca, 2)` here. That ratio
is what @sec-heterosis-relocation shows falling as the pools diverge, so the
number of testers a programme needs is not a constant of the crop: well
separated pools need fewer. Two limits. This is heterosis only -- the parental
additive contribution to testcross performance is not in $H$ and is not tested
here -- and it is one realisation of $d$ and one pool pair, so the ratio, and
with it every entry in @tbl-het-step6-testers, moves with the seed.

**Call.** `qr(model.matrix(...))$rank` on the layout you actually have, before
fitting anything; `heterosis_gca_sca()` only once the layout supports it.
**Check.** `sca_df > 0` if SCA is to be estimated; `residual_df > 0` if it is to
be tested.
**Warning sign.** A testcross file against one inbred tester per pool, analysed
as though it estimated SCA. It estimates
$\mu + g^A_i + (\text{that tester's contribution})$ and nothing else.
**Threshold.** Two testers to identify SCA. For ranking GCA, at this
$\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA_A}$ ratio of `r fmt(v_sca / v_gca, 2)` -- one
pool's GCA variance in the denominator, not the two-pool sum of
@sec-heterosis-relocation -- @eq-het-rho-k first exceeds $\rho_k = 0.85$ at
$k =$ `r min(which(1 / sqrt(1 + (v_sca / v_gca) * (nBt - seq_len(nBt)) / (seq_len(nBt) * (nBt - 1))) > 0.85))`
testers. At five testers the scan's mean is
`r fmt(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == 5], 4)`, which is
`r fmt((ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == 5] - 0.85) / (ts$cor_sd[ts$testers == 5] / sqrt(n_sets)), 1)`
standard errors of the mean of `r n_sets` sets above 0.85, while the s.d. over
tester sets at five testers is `r fmt(ts$cor_sd[ts$testers == 5], 3)`, so a single
set of five testers can fall on either side of 0.85. The scan puts the mean
correlation above 0.85 from five testers in this realisation, in agreement with the
closed form; ten testers give `r fmt(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == 10], 2)`. Recompute the requirement
when the ratio changes.

### Step 7 -- Fit the decomposition and check it reconstructs {#sec-heterosis-step7}

`heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)` is @eq-het-gca-sca-terms, not a model fit: it needs no
solver and returns $\mu$, `gca_A`, `gca_B` and the `sca` matrix. On simulated $d$
it must reconstruct every hybrid exactly, and the chunks in
@sec-heterosis-gca-sca assert that, together with the `lm()` interaction
equivalence, to `1e-9` times the largest $|H_{ij}|$ (the render stops if either fails).
On real data $d$ is unknown, so the route reverses: fit
`lm(H ~ factor(a) + factor(b))`, take the row and column effects as $g^A$ and
$g^B$ and the residual as $s_{ij}$. The two routes coincide only on a complete,
balanced factorial.

**Call.** `heterosis_gca_sca()` when $d$ is known (simulation); `lm()` with both
parent factors when it is not.
**Check.** The reconstruction residual, and that all three components are mean
zero.
**Warning sign.** A non-zero mean for `gca_A` or `sca`. The deviations are taken
from each pool's own line frequencies, so they sum to zero over that pool by
construction; a non-zero mean means the frequencies used were not the pool's.
**Threshold.** Machine precision for the reconstruction. **For the variance
components there is no threshold that transfers to a real pool**, and the
$\sqrt{2/n}$ figure quoted in @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is not one. It is one relative
standard deviation of the variance of $n$ **independent** observations, so even
for independent lines about a third of the GCA components falls outside it by
construction (`band_ind` in @tbl-het-step7-location), and it is valid only because the closed
forms are derived under the simulation's sampling model -- each line's genotype an
independent Bernoulli($p_k$) draw at every locus, hence unrelated lines and linkage
equilibrium within pool. A recycled heterotic pool satisfies neither: assumption
A3 (@sec-hp-cycle; declared in @sec-era-programme) makes within-pool recycling the
normal state of this system, so its lines share ancestors.

What a construction can measure is how the dispersion of the deviation of the
observed variance from its closed form changes when the lines are related, for the
part that founder sampling causes. Re-derive each pool as
`r book_cfg$n_pool_A` doubled haploids drawn from crosses among six of its own
members -- one Bernoulli draw per locus, so loci recombine freely and there is
**no physical linkage**, but the lines are related, and descent from six founders
induces linkage disequilibrium among them all the same. @tbl-het-step7-recycled
shows five such pairs of pools beside the independent lines, as an illustration of
what the deviations look like. The comparison that carries the inference follows
it (@tbl-het-step7-spread, @tbl-het-step7-location).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step7-recycled
#| tbl-cap: "Per cent deviation of the observed variance (divisor $n$) of each combining-ability component from its closed form (@eq-het-var-components). Rows draw1 to draw5: pairs of pools re-derived as 25 doubled haploids per pool from crosses among six founders of that pool (seeds 501 to 505); last row: the original, independently drawn lines. An illustration of single draws; the dispersion is in @tbl-het-step7-spread and @tbl-het-step7-location."
rel_dev <- function(A, B) {                     # % deviation, observed vs closed form
  p1 <- colMeans(A); p2 <- colMeans(B)
  cc <- heterosis_gca_sca(A, B, d)
  obs <- c(pvar(cc$gca_A), pvar(cc$gca_B), pvar(as.vector(cc$sca)))
  cf  <- c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p2)^2 * p1 * (1 - p1)),
           sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p1)^2 * p2 * (1 - p2)),
           4 * sum(d^2 * p1 * (1 - p1) * p2 * (1 - p2)))
  100 * (obs / cf - 1)
}
recycle <- function(W, n_found) {               # DH lines from crosses among founders
  fo <- W[sample.int(nrow(W), n_found), , drop = FALSE]
  t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(W)), function(i) {
    pr <- sample.int(n_found, 2)
    rbinom(ncol(W), 1, (fo[pr[1], ] + fo[pr[2], ]) / 2)
  }, numeric(ncol(W))))
}
dev <- t(vapply(seq_len(5), function(r) {
  set.seed(500 + r)                             # seeded per draw, not once
  rel_dev(recycle(U, 6), recycle(V, 6))
}, numeric(3)))
dimnames(dev) <- list(paste0("draw", seq_len(5)), c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA"))
tab7 <- rbind(dev, `independent lines` = rel_dev(U, V))
colnames(tab7) <- paste(colnames(tab7), "(%)")
fmt(tab7, 1)
```

Result 1. In the five draws the deviations range up to
`r sprintf("%.0f", max(abs(dev)))` % in absolute value; on the independently drawn
lines of the last row the three closed forms are within
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(abs(rel_dev(U, V))))` % of the observed variances. One draw
of each kind cannot show whether the recycled deviations are larger than those of
independent lines; the next two tables measure that.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step7-spread
#| tbl-cap: "Spread of the per cent deviation of @tbl-het-step7-recycled over replicated draws. `sd_rec`, `sd_ind`: standard deviation over replicates of the deviation, for pools re-derived from six founders and for independent Bernoulli lines at the same pool frequencies; `ratio`: `sd_rec / sd_ind`, with a bootstrap 95 % interval (`ratio_lo`, `ratio_hi`; 2000 resamples of replicates); `p_F`: p-value of an F test of equal variances (it assumes normal deviations, which is not checked), printed as `< 2e-16` when it is below the double-precision epsilon (the upper-tail probability, about 5e-55 for the SCA ratio, is representable, but `var.test` forms the two-sided value as 2 min(P, 1 - P) with the lower tail P rounded to 1, and so returns exactly 0). Location and tails of the same replicates are in @tbl-het-step7-location."
n_rep7 <- 1000
indep_lines <- function(n, p) matrix(rbinom(n * length(p), 1, rep(p, each = n)), n)
dev_rec <- t(vapply(seq_len(n_rep7), function(r) {
  set.seed(7000 + r)                            # seeded per replicate
  rel_dev(recycle(U, 6), recycle(V, 6))
}, numeric(3)))
dev_ind <- t(vapply(seq_len(n_rep7), function(r) {
  set.seed(8000 + r)
  rel_dev(indep_lines(nrow(U), pA), indep_lines(nrow(V), pB))
}, numeric(3)))
colnames(dev_rec) <- colnames(dev_ind) <- c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA")
band7 <- 100 * sqrt(2 / book_cfg$n_pool_A)
set.seed(1)                                     # bootstrap of the ratio of s.d.
boot_ratio <- replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(n_rep7, replace = TRUE); j <- sample(n_rep7, replace = TRUE)
  apply(dev_rec[i, ], 2, sd) / apply(dev_ind[j, ], 2, sd)
})
q95 <- apply(dev_ind, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
disp7 <- data.frame(
  sd_rec   = apply(dev_rec, 2, sd),  sd_ind = apply(dev_ind, 2, sd),
  ratio    = apply(dev_rec, 2, sd) / apply(dev_ind, 2, sd),
  ratio_lo = apply(boot_ratio, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  ratio_hi = apply(boot_ratio, 1, quantile, 0.975),
  p_F      = vapply(1:3, function(j) var.test(dev_rec[, j], dev_ind[, j])$p.value, 0),
  mean_rec = colMeans(dev_rec), mean_ind = colMeans(dev_ind),
  band_rec = colMeans(abs(dev_rec) > band7), band_ind = colMeans(abs(dev_ind) > band7),
  lo95_ind = q95[1, ], hi95_ind = q95[2, ],
  out95_rec = vapply(1:3, function(j)
    mean(dev_rec[, j] < q95[1, j] | dev_rec[, j] > q95[2, j]), 0))
tab_disp7 <- fmt(disp7, 3)
# fmt() would round a tiny p to 0; a p below machine epsilon prints as the floor, not as 0
tab_disp7$p_F <- format.pval(disp7$p_F, digits = 2, eps = .Machine$double.eps)
tab_disp7[, c("sd_rec", "sd_ind", "ratio", "ratio_lo", "ratio_hi", "p_F")]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-step7-location
#| tbl-cap: "Location and tails of the per cent deviation of @tbl-het-step7-recycled over the same replicates as @tbl-het-step7-spread. `mean_rec`, `mean_ind`: mean deviation, recycled and independent; `band_rec`, `band_ind`: share of replicates outside $\\pm 100\\sqrt{2/n}$ per cent; `lo95_ind`, `hi95_ind`: central 95 % range of the independent deviations, in per cent; `out95_rec`: share of recycled replicates outside that range."
tab_disp7[, c("mean_rec", "mean_ind", "band_rec", "band_ind", "lo95_ind", "hi95_ind",
              "out95_rec")]
```

Result 2. The comparison is `r n_rep7` recycled pairs of pools (seeds 7001 to
`r 7000 + n_rep7`) against `r n_rep7` independent sets of 25 lines per pool drawn as
Bernoulli at the pool frequencies of the original lines (seeds 8001 to
`r 8000 + n_rep7`). Over those replicates the standard deviation of the deviation is
larger for recycled pools than for independent lines in all three components: by a
factor of `r fmt(disp7["GCA_A", "ratio"], 2)` (95 % interval
`r fmt(disp7["GCA_A", "ratio_lo"], 2)` to `r fmt(disp7["GCA_A", "ratio_hi"], 2)`)
for `GCA_A`, `r fmt(disp7["GCA_B", "ratio"], 2)`
(`r fmt(disp7["GCA_B", "ratio_lo"], 2)` to `r fmt(disp7["GCA_B", "ratio_hi"], 2)`) for
`GCA_B` and `r fmt(disp7["SCA", "ratio"], 2)`
(`r fmt(disp7["SCA", "ratio_lo"], 2)` to `r fmt(disp7["SCA", "ratio_hi"], 2)`) for
`SCA`. Independent lines already fall outside the $\sqrt{2/n}$ band in
`r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_A", "band_ind"], 0)` % and
`r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_B", "band_ind"], 0)` % of replicates for the two GCA
components, against `r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_A", "band_rec"], 0)` % and
`r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_B", "band_rec"], 0)` % for recycled pools. Measured against
the central 95 % range of the independent deviations, recycled pairs fall outside
in `r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_A", "out95_rec"], 0)` %,
`r fmt(100 * disp7["GCA_B", "out95_rec"], 0)` % and
`r fmt(100 * disp7["SCA", "out95_rec"], 0)` % of replicates (`GCA_A`, `GCA_B`,
`SCA`), against the 5 % that independent lines give by construction. The mean
deviation of the recycled GCA components is below that of the independent ones
(`r sprintf("%.1f", disp7["GCA_A", "mean_rec"])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", disp7["GCA_B", "mean_rec"])` %
against `r sprintf("%.1f", disp7["GCA_A", "mean_ind"])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", disp7["GCA_B", "mean_ind"])` %; the standard error of each mean is about
`r fmt(max(disp7[c("GCA_A", "GCA_B"), "sd_rec"]) / sqrt(n_rep7), 1)` points).

Interpretation, and its limits. A tolerance calibrated on independent lines is too
narrow for related lines in this construction, most of all for the specific
component, whose dispersion is the one that grows most in relative terms
(`r fmt(disp7["SCA", "ratio"], 2)`-fold, against
`r fmt(disp7["GCA_A", "ratio"], 2)` and `r fmt(disp7["GCA_B", "ratio"], 2)`). Counting the components of the five-draw table that lie outside the
$\sqrt{2/n}$ band (`r sum(abs(dev) > 100 * sqrt(2 / book_cfg$n_pool_A))` of
`r length(dev)`, `r sum(abs(dev[, c("GCA_A", "GCA_B")]) > 100 * sqrt(2 / book_cfg$n_pool_A))`
of them in the GCA columns) would suggest that the GCA components carry the failure
and the SCA component does not. The count is not a measure, because the band is one
standard deviation and the independent comparison is a single draw; the replicated
comparison shows a larger dispersion in all three components. Why the dispersion grows is not tested. The closed forms, being sums of
per-locus terms, contain neither the covariance between loci across lines
(linkage disequilibrium, here induced by descent from few founders) nor the
relatedness between lines; the construction changes both at once and does not
separate them. A third candidate is the loss of segregating loci under six founders,
which changes the effective number of loci that the statistic averages. Each is a
candidate explanation, not a result. The inference
is limited to this construction: six founders, one doubled haploid per F1, free
recombination, 25 lines per pool, one $d$ and one pool pair, and a comparison
against independent Bernoulli lines at the pool frequencies, not against a
programme's own pedigree. A real recycled pool also carries disequilibrium that
physical linkage maintains across cycles, and the size of that contribution is not
measured anywhere in this book. The tolerance for a real pool must therefore be
recalibrated empirically on the programme's own pedigree; the closed forms remain
exact statements about the sampling model they are derived under.

### Step 8 -- Decide the $F_{ST}$ band on alignment, not on $F_{ST}$ {#sec-heterosis-step8}

The output of steps 4-7 answers one management question: should the pools be
pushed further apart? The chapter's answer is that $F_{ST}$ cannot inform it
(@sec-heterosis-flat: the total does not move in expectation) and that the quantity that can is
$\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ (@sec-heterosis-alignment: a factor of
`r round(max(al$total)/min(al$total), 2)` at constant $F_{ST}$, in the one
generating model of that section).

**Call.** $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ with the population divisor, alongside
$\bar d\,\overline{y^2}$; the two-term identity @eq-het-alignment is
the check.
**Check.** The sign and magnitude of the covariance relative to
$\bar d\,\overline{y^2}$.
**Warning sign.** A proposal to raise $F_{ST}$ justified by the divergence term
alone. Under neutral divergence the shared term pays for all of it, unit for
unit in expectation, and $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ falls at the same time.
**Threshold.** No universal one exists, and this chapter does not supply it: the
missing weight $\lambda$ between within- and between-pool diversity needs the
two covariances listed in @sec-heterosis-lambda, and this book estimates
neither.

## What this does not change

:::: {.callout-important}
## The diversity constraint stays additive

Nothing in this chapter reopens the optimisation. $\theta_S$, $GD_T$ and $\alpha$ are
computed on molecular coancestry and are functions of the frequencies alone; no
dominance term enters them, and @sec-ocs, @sec-combinatorial and @sec-advanced are
untouched. The combining-ability split of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca sits outside the
constraint for the same reason: it is a statement about the objective, not about
the feasible set.

A dominance model changes the **mean-performance ranking**, not the diversity
term. @sec-case-study states the same separation from the other side. Do not
conflate them, and do not read this chapter as licence to put a heterosis term
inside the constraint.
::::

What it does change is the interpretation of the constraint's output. By the
two-term identity @eq-het-alignment, the divergence term of a plan's
selected lines is $\tfrac{m}{2}[\bar d\,\overline{y^2} + \mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)]$,
and $GD_{BS}$ fixes only $\overline{y^2}$. Two plans with the same $\alpha$ and the
same $GD_{BS}$ therefore differ in that term by exactly $m/2$ times the difference
in their $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ (both computed on usage-weighted frequencies,
@sec-heterosis-step4), a quantity the partition does not contain and
only an estimate of $d$ can supply. How large that difference can be between two
*attainable* plans is not measured in this book. The scenario table,
@tbl-het-alignment, a factor of `r round(max(al$total)/min(al$total), 2)`
between its extremes, does not measure it: it holds one pool pair's frequencies
fixed and re-places $d$ across loci, which compares genetic architectures, while
a selection plan cannot move $d$ and changes only the selected lines'
frequencies, within what the candidate set and the budget on $\alpha$ allow.

### What it would take to use $d$ {#sec-heterosis-lambda}

@sec-catalogue, later, leaves a weight $\lambda$ undetermined between within- and
between-pool diversity and shows that, with expected heterosis as the objective,
$\lambda$ is $1/2$ under flat dominance and otherwise $\lambda_d$, a ratio of
two weighted means of $d$ (@eq-catalogue-lambda-d). This chapter can now say what would have to
be estimated to set it, and it is not much:

- **$\lambda$ needs two covariances, not $d$ itself.** Each weighted mean of $d$
  in $\lambda_d$ is $\bar d$ plus a covariance divided by a mean, as in
  @eq-het-alignment, so $\lambda_d$ needs $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ and
  $\mathrm{cov}(d, H_S)$, with $H_{S,k} = p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk}$ the
  within-pool heterozygosity of locus $k$, each relative to $\bar d$, on top of
  what the frequencies already give. A programme does not
  need per-locus dominance effects to weight the two diversity terms against
  each other; it needs to know whether its divergence is landing on its dominance
  loci.
- **Ranking crosses needs more.** $s_{ij}$ is a $d$-weighted inner product between
  two specific parents, so it needs the dominance effects locus by locus. This is the
  extension @sec-case-study names and the book does not attempt.
- **Fitting it needs a factorial, and a testcross file is not one.** The
  decomposition is the two-way layout with *identified* rows and columns, and
  against a single common tester no SCA is identifiable (@sec-heterosis-step6
  counts the degrees of freedom; @sec-mating-connectivity gives the general rank
  rule). Programmes that already cross two pools in a partial
  factorial for hybrid evaluation have the layout; programmes that testcross
  against one inbred tester per pool do not.

## Where this connects

@sec-subdivided supplied the partition and @sec-catalogue will use it; this chapter
supplies the reason the $GD_{BS}$ component is singled out for protection, and the
reason protecting it is not the same as maximising it. @sec-stages Trap 3, later,
recommends holding $F_{ST}$ in a band: @sec-heterosis-flat is why a band, and
@sec-heterosis-alignment is what to watch instead of the band.
@sec-heterosis-distance closes the loop with the coancestry kernel of
@sec-coancestry: under flat dominance, the diversity matrix and the heterosis
prediction are the same object.

@sec-genomic-prediction is the chapter this one supplies a missing term to. It
predicts breeding values with an additive model on a trait that is additive by
construction, and lists specific combining ability first among what it does not
model. @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is where that term comes from and
@sec-heterosis-relocation is what share of the variance in heterosis it holds;
both are derived here rather than fitted, because on a simulated $d$ they can be.

It also gives a reason why a heterotic *pattern* -- which pool crosses well onto
which -- is not recoverable from how far apart the pools have drifted:
@sec-heterosis-alignment's three scenarios share every frequency-based statistic
and differ by a factor of `r round(max(al$total)/min(al$total), 2)` in expected
heterosis in the generating model used here. @white2020 describe both the diversity
structure and the heterotic patterns of North American proprietary dent germplasm;
this chapter's reading is that the two cannot be recovered from one another.

Forward, the alignment result raises a question for the recurrent loop. Drift
moves frequencies independently of $d$, and selection on a line's own performance
cannot respond to $d$ either, because an inbred line's dominance contribution is
exactly zero (@sec-heterosis-id). That leaves selection on *cross* performance as
the only process of those considered here that can move frequencies in a way that
depends on where the dominance is, and it suggests that the alignment between
divergence and dominance is something each cycle either builds or erodes rather
than a standing asset; this is an inference from the algebra of this chapter, not
a result shown in it. A one-cycle constraint cannot see that, and neither can
$F_{ST}$. The loop on a dominance trait is run in @sec-alphasimr, which is the
pipeline this chapter's algebra describes. @sec-cycles runs selection under the
diversity budget on an additive index, with no dominance in the traits, and so
does not test the inference.

<!-- reproduce-chapter -->

## Reproduce this chapter {.unnumbered}

All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: [**05b-heterosis-dominance.R**](https://ederdbs.github.io/QG/downloads/05b-heterosis-dominance.R){download="05b-heterosis-dominance.R"}.
Download it, install `hybdiv`, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.
